bottom_line: Sound kitchen logic backed by a long cooking tradition, though no controlled taste test has been cited to confirm it on pizza.

text: Pizza has always changed with the cooks who make it, so a pizza topping invented in Canada in 1962 has as good a claim to the dish as the tomato, which reached Italy from the Americas.
bottom_line: A good answer to the claim that tradition rules pineapple out, but it says nothing about whether pineapple pizza tastes good.

text: Respected Italian pizza makers, including Gino Sorbillo in Naples and Franco Pepe in Caiazzo, have put pineapple pizzas on their own menus.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows skilled pizza makers think pineapple can work, though both rebuilt the recipe rather than copying the Canadian ham-and-pineapple version.

text: Italian pizzerias already serve pizzas with sweet fruit, such as figs with prosciutto, so a ban on fruit as a pizza topping is not a real Italian rule.
bottom_line: Fair point against a blanket 'no fruit' objection, but critics can still object to pineapple's particular sweetness and juice.

text: Whether a topping belongs on a pizza is decided by the person eating that pizza, so pineapple belongs on any pizza ordered by someone who wants it.
bottom_line: Strong as a point about personal choice, but it sidesteps the claim that cooks share standards about what makes food good.

text: In a YouGov poll of 1,000 U.S. adult citizens taken March 11-14, 2023, 22% said they love pineapple on pizza and 37% said they like it (59% positive), while 18% disliked it and 19% hated it (37% negative).
bottom_line: The clearest recent sign that most Americans accept pineapple on pizza, though a 2021 YouGov poll worded differently found more dislike than like.

text: A 2017 YouGov poll of Britons found 53% like pineapple on pizza and 41% dislike it, and only 15% of pizza lovers would ban it, fifth behind anchovies, olives and tuna.
bottom_line: Shows a narrow majority in favor in Britain, but the poll is nine years old and the margin is small.

text: Hawaiian pizza was the most popular pizza variety in Australia in 1999, at 15% of pizza sales.
bottom_line: Real buying behavior is better evidence than stated opinion, but the figure is old, from one country, and known only through a secondhand citation.

text: The next YouGov national poll of American adults on pizza toppings will find more people who like pineapple on pizza than people who dislike it.
Gino Sorbillo's pineapple pizza will still be on the menu at his Naples pizzeria at the end of 2026.
A controlled taste test finds that people rate a ham pizza with pineapple higher than the same ham pizza without pineapple.
A national poll finds that most Italians under 35 find pineapple on pizza acceptable.
Whether a food combination is good is decided mainly by whether the people eating it enjoy it, not by the rules of the cuisine it came from.
Pizza is a broad family of dishes that can change from country to country, not a single fixed Italian recipe.
Sweet and salty flavors can work together in a savory main dish, as they do in glazed ham or prosciutto with melon.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau posted in February 2017, "I have a pineapple. I have a pizza. And I stand behind this delicious Southwestern Ontario creation," in reply to the Icelandic president's remarks against pineapple on pizza.

Franco Pepe, the pizza maker of Pepe in Grani in Caiazzo, Italy, created AnaNascosta, a fried pizza with pineapple wrapped in San Daniele prosciutto, which won Dish of the Year 2019 at the Identità Golose event in Milan.
Pizza: A Global History, Carol Helstosky, 2008
bridge: Helstosky, a University of Denver historian, traces pizza from a cheap street food of eighteenth-century Naples to a global dish that took on new forms in every country it reached, which supports the view that pizza has always changed with the cooks who make it.
bottom_line: Solid history that undercuts the idea of one fixed true pizza, though it does not judge whether pineapple tastes good on one.

text: Pineapple generally releases juice as it bakes, which can leave the center of a thin-crust pizza wet and soggy.
bottom_line: A real kitchen problem, but cooks reduce it by draining or roasting the fruit first, so it argues for care rather than for keeping pineapple off pizza.

text: Italians, whose country gave the world modern pizza, reject pineapple on pizza by a wide margin, ranking it among the three worst things done to Italian food in a 2022 YouGov survey.
bottom_line: Carries weight on what pizza means in its home country, less on whether people elsewhere are wrong to enjoy it.

text: The syrup-sweet taste of canned pineapple makes a pizza taste more like dessert and covers up the tomato and cheese that a pizza is built around.
bottom_line: A common and honest complaint, but it is a matter of taste that the many people who like the pairing plainly do not share.

text: More American adults disliked pineapple on pizza than liked it in a large February 2021 YouGov poll, so pineapple is a pizza topping that splits a table rather than one that clearly belongs.
bottom_line: Meaningful, but a 2023 YouGov poll with different wording found the opposite balance, so the American evidence is mixed.

text: Neapolitan pizza, the style protected by a European Union quality label since 2010, has a short list of allowed ingredients that does not include pineapple.
bottom_line: Settles what may be sold as Neapolitan pizza, not what may go on pizza in general.

text: In a YouGov poll of 6,168 U.S. adults taken February 3-4, 2021, 35% said they dislike pineapple on pizza and 26% said they like it, making pineapple the fifth most disliked topping.
bottom_line: A large sample pointing the other way from the 2023 poll, which suggests question wording drives much of the American result.

text: In a 2022 YouGov survey across 17 countries, Italians ranked pineapple on pizza as the third worst thing that can be done to Italian food, with a net score of -63 (far more saying it is unacceptable than acceptable).
bottom_line: Strong evidence of what Italians think, though the article reports net scores rather than plain percentages.

text: In a 2019 YouGov survey, 24% of American pizza eaters named pineapple among their least favorite toppings, twice the 12% who named it among their top three favorites.
bottom_line: Shows pineapple draws more strong dislike than strong love, though disliking a topping is different from saying it does not belong on pizza at all.

text: A new YouGov poll of American adults will find more people dislike pineapple on pizza than like it, as the February 2021 YouGov poll did.
Most Italian pizzerias that added pineapple pizzas after 2023, including Gino Sorbillo's, will have dropped them from their menus.
A controlled taste test finds that even people who say they like pineapple on pizza rate a pineapple pizza lower than the same pizza without pineapple.
Sales data from major pizza chains show orders of pineapple pizzas falling steadily over a decade in the United States, Britain and Australia.
The country that created a dish has a special claim to define what properly goes on it.
Cooks share real standards of what makes food good, so a popular combination can still be a poor one.
A pizza is built around tomato, cheese and dough, so a topping that overpowers them works against the dish.

Icelandic President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson told students at a school in northern Iceland in February 2017 that he was opposed to pineapple on pizza and would ban it if he could, and later said the remark had gone too far.
You're doing Italian food all wrong, say Italians, YouGov, 2022
bridge: YouGov's 17-country survey found Italians ranked pineapple on pizza the third worst thing done to their cuisine, with a net score of -63, behind only ketchup on pasta and putting pasta in cold water before boiling.
bottom_line: Strong evidence of how pizza's home country sees the topping, weaker as a guide to what diners elsewhere should enjoy.

text: Commission Regulation (EU) No 97/2010 of 4 February 2010 entering a name in the register of traditional specialities guaranteed (Pizza Napoletana (TSG))
where_found: Official Journal of the European Union (EUR-Lex)
bridge: The regulation lists the ingredients a Pizza Napoletana may use (flour, yeast, water, tomatoes, salt, olive oil, garlic, oregano, basil and specific mozzarellas), and pineapple is not among them.
bottom_line: Decisive for what may be sold as Neapolitan pizza in the European Union, but it says nothing about pizza in general.

text: Watch Gordon Ramsay Suffer By Eating Pineapple Pizza, Time, 2017
bridge: Time reported that Gordon Ramsay ate a pineapple pizza for a children's hospital charity drive and called it a mistake and an Italian tragedy.
bottom_line: Shows a famous chef's distaste, but it is a staged charity stunt and one man's palate, so it deserves little weight as evidence.

text: Pizza eaters who like sweet and salty food need pizzerias to keep offering pineapple as a topping.
measured_by: The share of pizzerias that list pineapple as a topping and the share of pizza eaters who say they like it.
if_true: Both shares stay steady or rise.
if_false: Pizzerias drop pineapple and fewer people say they like it.
bottom_line: The largest group with a stake, about three in five American adults by the 2023 YouGov count.

text: Pizzeria owners in North America need toppings that most of their customers will order.
measured_by: Pineapple pizzas as a share of a pizzeria's orders.
if_true: Pineapple pizzas hold a steady share of orders.
if_false: Pineapple pizzas sell poorly and leave the menu.
bottom_line: Matters to every pizzeria, though no sales figures for pineapple have been cited.

text: Home cooks feeding families need to top a pizza with what their family likes without being mocked for it.
measured_by: The share of people in polls who say pineapple on pizza should be banned.
if_true: The share stays small, like the 15% of British pizza lovers in 2017.
if_false: The share grows and pineapple pizza becomes a mark of bad taste.
bottom_line: A light interest, since nobody can actually ban the topping.

text: Neapolitan pizza makers need the traditional recipe kept distinct from popular variations sold under the same name.
measured_by: Whether foreign versions of pizza are sold and described as Italian or Neapolitan.
if_true: Pineapple pizza spreads under the general name of pizza and the line between styles fades.
if_false: Pineapple pizza stays labeled as a Canadian or American variation, apart from Neapolitan pizza.
bottom_line: A real interest for a craft with legal protection, but it bears on labels more than on what anyone eats.

text: Diners who dislike sweet toppings need shared pizzas that do not put fruit on every slice.
measured_by: How often group orders include a pizza with no pineapple on it.
if_true: Pineapple ends up on more shared pizzas and some diners go without.
if_false: Group orders keep pineapple to separate pizzas or halves.
bottom_line: Covers more than a third of American adults by the 2023 YouGov count, but simple ordering habits meet the need.

text: Offering pineapple as a topping wins pizzerias orders from customers who would not order a pizza without it.
bottom_line: Plausible but unmeasured, since no sales study separating pineapple orders has been cited.

text: Treating pineapple pizza as normal food spares home cooks and children from being mocked for a harmless food choice.
bottom_line: A small but real social benefit; most of the mockery is in fun.

text: Selling ham-and-pineapple pizza around the world as ordinary pizza blurs what traditional Neapolitan pizza is, which can hurt pizza makers who sell the traditional style.
bottom_line: Hard to measure and probably small, since the European Union already protects the Neapolitan name.

text: The share of a nationally representative sample who say they like pineapple on pizza, minus the share who say they dislike it, is a fair measure of whether pineapple belongs on pizza as a matter of common taste.
Taste ratings given by people who eat the same pizza with and without pineapple, on a standard 1-to-9 liking scale, are a fair measure of whether pineapple improves a pizza.
Whether pineapple pizzas stay on the menus of well-known Italian pizzerias that added them is a fair measure of whether skilled pizza makers and their customers think pineapple belongs.
Many people who eat pizza enjoy pizza topped with pineapple.
Enjoyment by the people eating a food is the right test of whether an ingredient belongs on that food.
Pineapple can be cooked on a pizza without ruining the crust, cheese or tomato.
Pizzerias in North America keep pineapple on their topping lists and keep offering ham and pineapple pizza as a standard choice.
More Italian pizza makers add their own pineapple pizzas to tasting menus, following Franco Pepe and Gino Sorbillo.
Pineapple pizza is treated as an ordinary regional style of pizza, like Chicago deep dish, rather than as a joke or an insult to Italian food.
The share of Italians who rank pineapple on pizza among the worst things done to their food falls in later surveys.
Pineapple is one of the best toppings that can be put on a pizza.
Pineapple pizza deserves the same standing as Neapolitan pizza and should be served in pizzerias in Naples.
Pineapple on pizza is acceptable for people who enjoy it, even if it is not a traditional Italian topping.
Pineapple can work on pizza when it is prepared carefully, such as drained or roasted and paired with salty meat.
Tipping in American restaurants should be replaced by higher menu prices and higher wages.
bottom_line: The evidence that tips track service only weakly and carry customer bias is solid and replicated. The evidence that many diners and servers dislike losing tips is just as solid, from falling Yelp ratings to Joe's Crab Shack returning 14 of 18 restaurants to tipping. The real fight is over who should carry the risk of a slow night, and whether a restaurant can post a higher menu price without losing customers to places that leave the tip off the menu.
hook: When diners rated service perfect, white servers' tips rose from 16.8 to 23.4 percent of the bill, but Black servers got 16.6 percent either way (Lynn and colleagues, Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 2008).
question: Should American restaurants stop asking for tips and instead build the cost of service into menu prices and pay their staff higher wages?
ask: The page most needs a study comparing servers' total pay, tips included, before and after a U.S. restaurant switched to service-included pricing.

text: Tip size in American restaurants tracks the quality of service only weakly, so tipping does a poor job of rewarding good servers.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because two meta-analyses of dozens of studies agree the link is real but small, which undercuts tipping's main defense.

text: Customer tipping in American restaurants lets diners' racial biases help set servers' pay.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because the tip gap for Black servers has turned up in several studies that controlled for rated service quality, though the gap is modest in size.

text: Waitstaff and bartenders who depend on tips have unpredictable paychecks that can collapse in a slow week or a bad season.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because income swings are real for tipped workers, but higher fixed wages can bring fewer hours, so steadiness is not guaranteed.

text: Tipping in American restaurants sends most of the money diners pay for service to dining-room staff and leaves cooks and dishwashers with little of it.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the split is real in many restaurants, but federal rules since 2018 let restaurants that pay the full minimum wage pool tips with kitchen staff, so tipping itself is not the only fix.

text: Servers whose income depends on tips have to put up with customer harassment to protect their earnings.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the main survey behind the claim is large and specific but comes from an advocacy group and compares wage rules rather than tipping versus no tipping.

text: Restaurants in most other wealthy countries build service into menu prices and still deliver good service.
bottom_line: Modest weight, because it shows service-included pricing can work, but those countries also differ in health care, labor law and dining habits, so the comparison is loose.

text: A meta-analysis of 13 studies covering 2,547 dining parties at 20 restaurants found an average correlation of only .11 between tip size and diners' ratings of service.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because it pools many independent studies and a later, larger meta-analysis found a similarly small link.

text: A meta-analysis of 74 studies with 12,271 people found a small positive relation between service quality and percent tipped (r = .15) and found racial minority servers were tipped less than white servers (Cohen's d = .17).
bottom_line: Strong weight, because it is the broadest summary of the research, though the same paper also finds service quality is the best single predictor of tips.

text: In one restaurant study, white servers' tips rose from 16.8 percent of the bill for less than perfect service to 23.4 percent for perfect service, while Black servers received 16.6 percent either way.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it controls for rated service and was itself a replication, but it is one set of restaurants and the size of the gap varies across studies.

text: Among waitstaff and bartenders, 18.0 percent were in poverty in states with the $2.13 federal tipped wage, compared with 10.2 percent in states that pay tipped workers the full minimum wage.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the gap is large, but it compares states that differ in many ways and is about the tipped wage floor rather than ending tipping.

text: Restaurants that adopt service-included pricing will report lower staff turnover than similar tipping restaurants in the same city.
Food-service employment in Chicago will keep pace with the national food-service trend as the city's tipped wage moves toward the full minimum wage.
A study finds that servers' total pay held steady or rose at American restaurants that switched from tipping to service-included pricing.
A study using post-2020 data finds that customer ratings and visits did not fall at American restaurants after they replaced tipping with higher menu prices.
Diners in the United States will keep eating out at about the same rate when restaurant menu prices rise by roughly the amount they used to leave as a tip.
Restaurant owners who stop collecting tips will pass the extra menu revenue on to workers as wages instead of keeping it as profit.
A server's pay should depend mainly on the employer and the work done, not on the moods and biases of individual customers.

Amanda Cohen, chef and owner of the New York restaurant Dirt Candy, ended tipping when Dirt Candy reopened in 2015 and has said that paying staff a steady wage protects them from slow nights and customers who tip poorly.
Brian Palmer argued in his July 2013 Slate column "Tipping Is an Abomination" that tipping in American restaurants is bad for diners, servers and restaurants and should be abolished.
Black-White Earnings Gap among Restaurant Servers: A Replication, Extension, and Exploration of Consumer Racial Discrimination in Tipping, by Zachary W. Brewster and Michael Lynn (2014)
bridge: An exit survey of 394 restaurant customers found that both white and Black diners tipped Black servers less than white servers, with no sign that the gap came from differences in service skill.
bottom_line: Strong weight on whether tips carry racial bias into pay, though one survey of diners in one region is a narrow base.

text: The Glass Floor: Sexual Harassment in the Restaurant Industry, by Restaurant Opportunities Centers United and Forward Together (2014)
bridge: A survey of 688 current and former restaurant workers in 39 states reports that tipped workers tolerate harassment from customers whose tips they depend on.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the sample is large and the link to tips is specific, but the authors are advocates for ending the subminimum tipped wage.

text: Tipping Is an Abomination, by Brian Palmer (2013)
bridge: Palmer argues that tipping is bad for diners, bad for servers and bad for restaurants, that it perpetuates racism, and that tip size has little to do with the quality of the work.
bottom_line: Modest weight, because it is an opinion column that gathers the research of others rather than adding new findings.

text: Most American diners would rather keep tipping than pay higher menu prices to get rid of it.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because surveys and real restaurant trials point the same way, and a restaurant reform that customers reject does not last.

text: Experienced servers at busy American restaurants earn more from tips than most restaurants could afford to pay them as a flat wage.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it is true for high-volume and high-check dining rooms and explains why many servers oppose the change, but it says little about servers at slow or cheap restaurants.

text: Tipping lets American diners pay more for good service and less for bad service.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because service quality is the strongest single predictor of tip size, even though the link is weak in absolute terms.

text: Replacing tips with wages would cost American restaurant servers the federal tax deduction on up to $25,000 of tip income that runs through 2028.
bottom_line: Modest weight, because the deduction is real and current law, but it is temporary and does not touch payroll taxes.

text: Small independent American restaurants would carry the risk of switching to higher fixed wages that large chains can spread across many locations.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because a single restaurant that loses customers after a price change has no other locations to absorb it, though this argues for an industry-wide rule more than against the idea.

text: Joe's Crab Shack tested no tipping at 18 restaurants with a $12 minimum hourly wage and menu prices raised less than 20 percent, found 60 percent of customers disliked the change, and returned 14 of the 18 to tipping.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it is a real market test by a mid-priced chain, but it is one company's internal survey reported secondhand.

text: Massachusetts voters rejected Question 5 in 2024, which would have phased out the lower tipped minimum wage while still allowing tips, by 64.13 percent to 35.87 percent.
bottom_line: Modest weight, because it is a large real vote, but the measure was about the wage floor and kept tipping, so it tests the higher-wage half of the belief more than the end of tipping.

text: Most U.S. restaurants that publicly drop tipping between 2026 and 2029 will bring tipping back within three years.
A new within-restaurant study using post-2020 data will again find that customer ratings fall after a restaurant replaces tipping with higher menu prices.
A study finds that diners at American no-tipping restaurants rate service quality lower than diners at matched tipping restaurants.
A study finds that experienced servers left American no-tipping restaurants for tipping restaurants at higher rates than they left tipping restaurants.
Diners judge restaurant prices by the number printed on the menu, not by the total they end up paying after the tip.
Customers are better placed than restaurant managers to judge and reward good table service night by night.
The best-paid servers at busy restaurants would lose more under a fixed wage than lower-paid restaurant workers would gain.

Danny Meyer, chief executive of Union Square Hospitality Group, brought tipping back to his restaurants in July 2020, writing that "it's the inability to share tips that is the problem, not the tips themselves."

Joshua Chaisson, a Maine server who cofounded Restaurant Workers of America, has campaigned to keep the tip credit, saying that when Maine raised servers' base wage, diners questioned whether they still needed to tip and his income would have fallen.
Tom Colicchio, chef and owner of Craft in New York, dropped tipping at Craft's lunch service in 2015 and later wrote publicly that the experiment "didn't work."
Tipping Culture in America: Public Sees a Changed Landscape, by Pew Research Center (2023)
bridge: In a national survey, 72% of U.S. adults said they oppose businesses adding automatic service charges or tips to customers' bills, which shows how many diners resist losing control over the service payment.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the sample is large and national, but the question asked about added service charges rather than higher menu prices with no tip.

text: Danny Meyer's restaurant group eliminates no-tipping policy, by Restaurant Dive (2020)
bridge: The article reports that Union Square Hospitality Group dropped its five-year Hospitality Included policy, that many experienced front-of-house workers had left after the 2015 switch, and that Meyer concluded the inability to share tips was the problem rather than tips themselves.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because it is the best-known American trial of the idea, but the reversal came during the 2020 pandemic, which muddies what caused it.

text: Waitstaff and bartenders at slow or low-priced restaurants need a steady paycheck that covers rent in a bad week.
measured_by: Week-to-week variation in take-home pay and the poverty rate among waitstaff and bartenders.
if_true: Pay swings narrow and the poverty rate falls where service is priced into the menu.
if_false: Pay swings narrow only by cutting hours, and the poverty rate does not fall.
bottom_line: Strong interest, because tipped workers at the low end carry most of the income risk under tipping.

text: Black servers need pay that does not depend on customers' racial bias.
measured_by: The gap in hourly pay between Black and white servers doing comparable work.
if_true: The gap shrinks toward zero when pay is set by wage rather than by tips.
if_false: The gap persists through hiring, shift assignment or section placement even without tips.
bottom_line: Strong interest, because the tip gap is documented, though wage pay can carry bias through other routes.

text: Restaurant cooks and dishwashers need a fair share of what diners pay for a meal.
measured_by: Kitchen workers' hourly pay compared with dining-room workers' total pay in the same restaurant.
if_true: The kitchen-to-dining-room pay gap narrows after service is priced into the menu.
if_false: The gap stays the same or kitchen pay falls as customers leave.
bottom_line: Moderate interest, because the split is real but tip pooling under current law can address part of it.

text: Experienced servers at busy restaurants need to keep tip earnings that often exceed what a flat wage would pay.
measured_by: Total hourly pay, tips included, for servers at high-volume and high-priced restaurants.
if_true: Their total pay holds steady after a switch because menu prices fund comparable wages.
if_false: Their total pay falls and many move to restaurants that still allow tips.
bottom_line: Strong interest, because these servers are the most organized voice against ending tips and have the most to lose.

text: Owners of small independent restaurants need menu prices that do not look higher than their competitors'.
measured_by: Customer counts and profit margins after a switch, compared with nearby tipping restaurants.
if_true: Customer counts recover once diners learn that menu prices include service.
if_false: Customers shift to competitors whose menus look cheaper, and margins fall.
bottom_line: Strong interest, because a single restaurant that switches alone bears the whole price-comparison risk.

text: Diners need a way to reward good service and hold back money for bad service.
measured_by: Diners' reported satisfaction and sense of control over what they pay, by tipping policy.
if_true: Satisfaction stays level because managers, not tips, enforce service quality.
if_false: Satisfaction falls because diners feel they lost a say over service.
bottom_line: Moderate interest, because diners value the control, even though measured tips respond to service only weakly.

text: Replacing tips with steady wages would lower the poverty rate among American waitstaff and bartenders.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the 7.8-point gap comes from EPI's comparison of states with different tipped wage floors, not from ending tipping itself, so the true effect could be smaller.

text: Ending tipping in American restaurants would remove the tip gap Black servers face for the same rated service.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the 6.8-point figure is the largest gap in one study (23.4 versus 16.6 percent), while meta-analysis puts the average gap as small.

text: Pricing service into American menus would let restaurants pay cooks and dishwashers more out of the same customer spending.
bottom_line: Modest weight, because the money can be shifted, but no source here measures how much kitchen pay actually rose where tipping ended.

text: Service-included pricing at American restaurants would put off a large share of customers who prefer to tip.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the 60 percent comes from one chain's 2016 trial, but it matches survey and ratings research.

text: Flat wages would cut take-home pay for servers at busy, high-priced American restaurants.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because the loss is real for top earners, but no source here measures its typical size.

text: Replacing tips with wages would take away American servers' federal deduction on tip income through 2028.
bottom_line: Modest weight, because $25,000 is the cap rather than the typical tax saving, and the deduction expires after 2028.

text: Ending tipping in American restaurants would take away diners' main way to pay more for good service and less for bad.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, because most diners say they use tips this way (Pew 2023), though measured tips respond to service only weakly.

text: Servers' total hourly pay, tips included, at restaurants that switch to service-included pricing, compared with similar tipping restaurants in the same city, is a fair measure of whether replacing tips helps servers.

Customer counts and online ratings at restaurants that drop tipping, compared with similar restaurants that keep it, over two years, is a fair measure of whether diners accept higher menu prices in place of tips.

Restaurant employment in cities that raise tipped workers to the full minimum wage, compared with the national restaurant trend, is a fair measure of whether higher wages in place of tips cost restaurant jobs.
Tipping in American restaurants produces worse outcomes for workers, such as biased, unstable or unequal pay, than wages funded by menu prices would.
American restaurants can raise menu prices enough to fund higher wages without losing so many customers that the change fails.
Restaurant workers' pay should be set by employers as a wage rather than by customers as a gift.
Menu prices at restaurants that drop tipping rise by roughly 15% to 20%, the share diners used to add as a tip.
Some experienced servers at busy, high-priced restaurants leave for restaurants that still allow tipping.
Pay gaps between dining-room and kitchen workers in American restaurants narrow as service money is paid out as wages to the whole staff.
American diners come to read menu prices as the full price of a meal, as diners in most of Europe and Japan already do.
Federal law should ban tipping in all American restaurants and require every restaurant to pay workers fixed wages.
Tipping for every kind of service in the United States, from taxis to hair salons, should be abolished.
American restaurants should be allowed to replace tipping with higher menu prices and higher wages if they choose to.
The lower tipped minimum wage in American restaurants should be raised to the full minimum wage while tipping continues.
Working from home is better for most office workers than working in an office.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that home days save office workers about an hour of commuting and that a hybrid schedule cuts quitting without hurting performance. It is thin and mixed on working from home every day, where good studies show losses in mentoring, promotion, wellbeing and, in some jobs, output. Much of the fight is over whether "working from home" means some days or all days, and whether "better" means a worker's daily life or a worker's career.
hook: On each day they work from home, office workers across 27 countries save an average of 72 minutes they would otherwise spend commuting (Aksoy, Barrero, Bloom, Davis, Dolls and Zarate, 2023).
question: Is working from home better for most office workers than working in an office?
ask: The page most needs a long-run study comparing promotion and pay for fully remote and fully in-office workers in the same jobs, so the career question stops resting on two Chinese trials.

text: Office workers who work from home skip a daily commute that averaged 72 minutes on home days across 27 countries, time they can put toward sleep, family or the job itself.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the time saving is the largest, best-measured and least disputed gain of working from home, though it shrinks for people who live near the office.

text: Office workers who are allowed to work from home part of the week quit their jobs less often than office workers who must come in every day.
bottom_line: Strong weight, because it rests on a randomized trial of 1,612 employees, but the trial tested two home days a week, not working from home full-time.

text: Working from home lets office workers who are parents or caregivers handle school pickups, sick children and appointments without taking a day off.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: large surveys show most home workers say their work-life balance improved, but the gain depends on having a workable space at home.

text: Office workers with long commutes, and women and non-managers, gain the most from working from home because the daily trip to the office costs them the most.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the Trip.com trial found its biggest drops in quitting in these groups, which supports the claim for many workers but not for every one.

text: Most office workers who can work from home say they would give up some pay to keep that option, which means they themselves judge it better than the office.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a stated willingness to pay is good evidence of what workers value, but survey answers can differ from what people actually do.

text: A quiet home office can raise output on focused, individual work, as Ctrip call center workers at home handled more calls per minute than their office peers.
bottom_line: Some weight: the finding comes from a careful trial, but from one routine job in 2010 to 2011, so it may not hold for collaborative office work.

text: In a randomized trial of 1,612 employees at Trip.com, working from home two days a week cut quitting by one third and made no detectable difference to performance reviews or promotions.
bottom_line: The strongest single finding for the belief, though it tested hybrid work at one Chinese technology firm.

text: Ctrip call center employees randomly assigned to work from home for nine months performed 13 percent better and quit at half the rate of the office group, but were promoted less often for the same performance.
bottom_line: Good evidence that home work suits routine, individual jobs, cut by its own finding of a promotion penalty.

text: Across 27 countries, workers saved an average of 72 minutes of commuting on each day they worked from home, and spent about 40 percent of that time on their jobs and about 11 percent on caregiving.
bottom_line: A large, cross-country estimate of the clearest benefit, based on what workers report rather than measured travel.

text: A majority of remote-capable U.S. employees will still work from home at least part of the week despite return-to-office orders at large employers.
A new randomized trial of office workers will find that workers assigned to work from home quit less often than those assigned to the office, with no drop in performance ratings.
A multi-year randomized trial finds that fully remote office workers are promoted at the same rate as in-office peers with equal performance.
A study of junior office workers finds that structured online mentoring closes the feedback gap between teams that sit together and teams that work remotely.
Whether working from home is better for an office worker should be judged mainly by the worker's own time, wellbeing and job satisfaction, not only by the employer's output.
Most office workers have a home setup, such as a quiet room and reliable internet, good enough to work there for much of the week.
The losses of working from home, such as slower mentoring and fewer chance contacts, can be made up with planned in-person days, video calls and deliberate coaching.

Brian Chesky, chief executive of Airbnb, announced in April 2022 that Airbnb employees could live and work anywhere, working from home or the office as suited them, after the company had what he called its most productive two years while working remotely.

Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom said in 2024, on publishing his Trip.com trial in Nature, that hybrid work with two days at home is a "win-win-win" for employee productivity, performance and retention.
Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance, Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han and James Liang, 2024
bridge: A randomized trial of 1,612 Trip.com employees found that two home days a week cut resignations by about a third with no measurable loss in performance reviews or promotions over two years.
bottom_line: Heavy weight for hybrid work, because it is a large randomized trial in a professional workforce, but it tested two home days a week rather than working from home every day.

text: Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment, Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts and Zhichun Jenny Ying, 2015
bridge: Ctrip call center workers randomly assigned to work from home performed better and quit less than their office peers, though they were promoted less often.
bottom_line: Strong weight as the first careful trial of full-time home work, limited by covering one routine job before the pandemic.

text: Why Working from Home Will Stick, Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom and Steven J. Davis, 2021
where_found: National Bureau of Economic Research, Working Paper 28731
bridge: Large repeated surveys of American workers found that most valued the option to work from home, many as much as a pay raise, and that saved commuting time was the main gain.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: strong on what workers say they value, weaker on whether working from home actually leaves them better off.

text: Junior office workers learn their jobs more slowly when they work from home because they get less informal feedback from experienced colleagues sitting nearby.
bottom_line: Strong weight for young workers: engineers who sat with their teammates got 22 percent more comments on their code, mostly flowing to juniors, though the effect matters less for veterans.

text: Office workers who work from home are promoted less often than office-based peers with the same performance.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the Ctrip trial found exactly that, but the later Trip.com hybrid trial found no promotion gap, so the cost may depend on how many days are spent at home.

text: Fully remote office workers say they are thriving in their lives less often than hybrid workers or office workers whose jobs could be done remotely.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Gallup's 2025 figures show a real gap (36 percent versus 42 percent) in a huge sample, but survey data cannot rule out that people who choose remote work differ to begin with.

text: Working from home blurs the line between job and home, so many office workers end up working longer hours, including more hours outside normal business hours.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a study of more than 10,000 IT professionals found hours outside normal business hours rose 18 percent, though that was during the pandemic, with schools closed.

text: Hybrid work, rather than working from home every day, is what most of the strongest evidence supports, so the claim that working from home beats the office overstates the studies.
bottom_line: Heavy weight as a limit on the claim: the best trial tested two home days a week, and the fully remote group does worse than hybrid on several wellbeing measures.

text: When a whole company works remotely, office workers' collaboration networks become more siloed, cutting the cross-team contacts that new ideas and career moves depend on.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a study of Microsoft employees showed the effect clearly, but it measured collaboration patterns, not workers' own wellbeing or pay.

text: Data entry workers in India randomly assigned to work from home were 18 percent less productive than those assigned to the office, with about two thirds of the gap appearing on the first day.
bottom_line: Strong design, but it measures output for the employer in one low-wage job in India rather than how workers' own lives fare.

text: Before offices closed, software engineers whose whole team sat in one building received 22 percent more comments on their code than engineers on teams split across buildings, and the gap mostly vanished once everyone went remote.
bottom_line: Good evidence that sitting together helps junior workers learn, from one Fortune 500 firm.

text: Among more than 10,000 IT professionals at an Asian company, working from home during the pandemic raised hours worked, including 18 percent more outside normal business hours, while productivity fell 8 to 19 percent.
bottom_line: Moderate weight, since pandemic conditions such as closed schools may explain part of the drop.

text: Only 36 percent of fully remote employees said they were thriving in their lives, compared with 42 percent of hybrid workers and 42 percent of on-site workers whose jobs could be done remotely.
bottom_line: A large-sample warning about full-time home work, though it cannot separate the effect of remote work from who chooses it.

text: A long-run study will find that office workers who worked fully remotely early in their careers earned less or were promoted less five years later than comparable in-office peers.
Gallup's State of the Global Workplace reports will keep showing fully remote employees thriving in their lives at lower rates than hybrid and on-site remote-capable employees.
A large randomized trial finds that office workers assigned to work from home full-time report lower life satisfaction after one year than those assigned to the office.
Repeats of the Trip.com hybrid trial at U.S. and European firms find that working from home has no effect on quit rates.
Learning, mentoring and career growth that come from sitting near colleagues matter to most office workers more than the hours they save by not commuting.
Workers' stated preference for working from home is not a reliable guide to what leaves them better off over a whole career.
Findings from part-time hybrid arrangements cannot be stretched to show that working from home full-time is better than the office.

Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JPMorgan Chase, ordered most of the bank's employees back to the office five days a week starting in 2025 and told young workers in May 2025 that "you can't learn working from your basement."

Andy Jassy, chief executive of Amazon, wrote in a September 2024 memo ordering corporate staff back to the office five days a week that "the advantages of being together in the office are significant," citing easier learning, collaboration and invention.
The Power of Proximity to Coworkers, Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais, 2023
where_found: National Bureau of Economic Research, Working Paper 31880 (later published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2026)
bridge: Software engineers at a Fortune 500 firm who sat in the same building as their teammates got more feedback on their code, with the gains going mostly to younger and newer engineers, while experienced engineers wrote less code.
bottom_line: Strong weight on the cost of remote work to junior workers' learning, from a clever natural experiment at one firm, though it says less about veteran workers.

text: The effects of remote work on collaboration among information workers, Longqi Yang, David Holtz, Sonia Jaffe and others, 2022
bridge: When Microsoft moved its US employees to firm-wide remote work, their collaboration networks became more static and siloed, with fewer ties across groups and more asynchronous communication.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a very large dataset showing a real change in how people work together, but it measured collaboration patterns, not whether workers were better or worse off.

text: Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from Personnel and Analytics Data on Information Technology Professionals, Michael Gibbs, Friederike Mengel and Christoph Siemroth, 2023
bridge: More than 10,000 IT professionals at an Asian services firm worked longer hours after moving home in 2020, including more hours outside business hours, while their measured output per hour fell.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: careful use of company data, but recorded during the pandemic, with schools closed and no time to adjust.

text: Parents of young children need predictable hours and time at home to handle school pickups and sick days.
measured_by: Share of working parents who say their job lets them balance work and family, from surveys such as Pew's.
if_true: The share is higher among parents who work from home than among parents in the office.
if_false: The share is no higher, or lower, among parents who work from home.
bottom_line: A strong interest, well matched to the commuting and flexibility gains, though parents of small children at home also reported larger productivity drops during the pandemic.

text: Office workers with long commutes need their travel time back for sleep, family and rest.
measured_by: Minutes of commuting saved per week and how those minutes are spent, from time-use surveys.
if_true: Saved minutes go mostly to rest, family and the job, and long commuters quit less when allowed home days.
if_false: Saved minutes are swallowed by longer work hours and quit rates do not change.
bottom_line: The clearest interest on this side, because the time saved is large and easy to measure.

text: Office workers with disabilities or chronic illnesses need jobs they can do without a daily trip to an office.
measured_by: Employment rate of people with disabilities in office occupations.
if_true: Their employment rate rises where working from home is widely offered.
if_false: Their employment rate does not change with access to remote work.
bottom_line: A real interest whose size this page has not yet sourced; it needs a figure before it can carry much weight.

text: Junior employees early in their careers need regular, close contact with experienced colleagues to learn the job and get noticed for promotion.
measured_by: Feedback received, skill growth and promotion rates of junior employees by work arrangement.
if_true: Junior remote workers get as much feedback and are promoted as often as junior office workers.
if_false: Junior remote workers get less feedback and are promoted more slowly.
bottom_line: The strongest interest against the belief, backed by the code-feedback and Ctrip promotion findings.

text: Office workers who live alone need daily in-person contact with other people to avoid loneliness.
measured_by: Daily loneliness and thriving rates among workers who live alone, by work arrangement.
if_true: Remote workers who live alone report loneliness no more often than office workers who live alone.
if_false: Remote workers who live alone report loneliness more often.
bottom_line: A real concern given Gallup's lower thriving rates for fully remote workers, but hybrid schedules may meet it without daily office attendance.

text: Downtown restaurant, cafe and shop owners need office workers in city centers on weekdays to stay in business.
measured_by: Weekday foot traffic and sales in downtown business districts.
if_true: Downtown weekday sales stay below their pre-2020 level where working from home is common.
if_false: Downtown sales recover fully despite widespread working from home.
bottom_line: A genuine interest, but it concerns third parties rather than whether working from home is better for the office workers themselves.

text: Office workers who work from home get back the time they would have spent commuting on each home day.
bottom_line: The 72-minute figure is an average across 27 countries; the gain is largest for long commuters and close to zero for people who live next to the office.

text: Office workers given the option to work from home part of the week quit their jobs less often.
bottom_line: Taken from the Trip.com trial, where the drop was largest among long commuters, women and non-managers; it holds for hybrid work, not proven for full-time home work.

text: Office workers who are parents spend part of the commuting time they save on caregiving.
bottom_line: An estimate from the finding that about 11 percent of the 72 minutes saved goes to caregiving; parents living with children were found to put more of their savings into care, so this is likely low for them.

text: Junior office workers who work away from their teammates receive less feedback on their work from experienced colleagues.
bottom_line: Measured for software engineers at one firm; the size for other office jobs is unknown, but the direction is consistent with the Ctrip promotion penalty.

text: Office workers who work from home full-time say they are thriving in their lives less often than hybrid or on-site workers.
bottom_line: Gallup's 2025 gap of 36 versus 42 percent is real in a large sample, but it may partly reflect who chooses fully remote work.

text: Fewer office workers in city centers on weekdays means less business for the shops and restaurants that serve them.
bottom_line: The direction is plain, but no source read for this page gives a figure, so the size is left blank until someone adds one.

text: The quit rate of office workers randomly assigned to work from home, compared with office workers in the same jobs randomly assigned to the office, is a fair measure of which arrangement workers themselves find better.
Promotion and pay growth over five years for remote and in-office workers with equal starting performance is a fair measure of whether working from home costs office workers their careers.
The share of workers who say they are thriving, compared by work arrangement within the same jobs, is a fair measure of whether working from home makes office workers' lives better.
Office workers who work from home save substantial time and money by skipping the daily commute.
Working from home does not cost most office workers enough in learning, promotion or social connection to cancel out its gains.
An office worker's own wellbeing, time and satisfaction are the right test of whether a work arrangement is better for that worker.
Office workers given home days would spend less time and money commuting within the first year.
Employers that allow office workers to work from home part of the week would see fewer resignations within a year or two.
Over a decade, widespread working from home would leave downtown office buildings emptier and push some office workers to move to cheaper towns farther from their employers.
Over a decade, young office workers who started their careers mostly at home would show whether remote starts slow pay growth and promotion compared with careers begun in an office.
Working from home full-time is better for nearly every office worker than any arrangement that requires coming into an office.
Working from home two or three days a week is better for most office workers than working in an office every day.
Office workers should be allowed to choose whether to work from home for part of the week.
Smartphones and social media are the main cause of the rise in teenage anxiety and depression since 2012.
bottom_line: The rise in American teen depression and sadness since about 2012 is well documented, and experiments and natural experiments show social media can lower mood somewhat; what remains contested is whether those effects are big enough to make smartphones and social media the main cause rather than one cause among several. The fight is really over the word "main": correlations are small, the best causal studies are mostly in young adults, and teen-specific results from Australia's ban and longer trials are only now arriving.
hook: In 2023, 40% of American high school students said they had felt so sad or hopeless for two weeks or more that they stopped some usual activities, up from 30% in 2013 (CDC, Youth Risk Behavior Survey Data Summary and Trends Report 2013 to 2023).
question: Are smartphones and social media the main reason teenage anxiety and depression have risen since 2012, or just one cause among several?
ask: This page most needs a teen-specific causal result, such as the published evaluation of Australia's under-16 social media ban, that measures depression or self-harm rather than mood alone.

text: The sharp rise in depression and anxiety among American teenagers began around 2012, the same years most American teenagers came to own smartphones with front cameras and social media apps.
bottom_line: The timing fits well and is the backbone of the case, but timing alone cannot rule out other causes that arrived in the same years.

text: Natural experiments, such as the staggered arrival of Facebook at American colleges between 2004 and 2006, show student mental health getting worse at colleges where Facebook arrived compared with colleges where it had not yet arrived.
bottom_line: This is some of the strongest causal evidence available because the arrival dates were not chosen by the students, though it studies college students on early Facebook, not teenagers on today's phones.

text: Randomized trials in which people quit or sharply cut social media for a few weeks generally find small improvements in mood, anxiety or life satisfaction.
bottom_line: Experiments are the right tool for a causal question, but the measured gains are small and mostly in young adults, so they support a real effect more than they support social media being the main cause.

text: Teenage girls, who spend the most time on image-based social media apps, show a much larger rise in depression, sadness and self-harm since 2012 than teenage boys, which is the pattern a social comparison cause would produce.
bottom_line: The sex difference fits the social media account well, though girls also report higher rates of depression in eras before smartphones, so the gap needs the trend, not just the level, to carry weight.

text: Smartphones in teenagers' hands push out sleep, in-person time with friends and physical activity, each of which protects teenagers against depression on its own.
bottom_line: Each displaced activity is well supported as protective, so this gives a plausible route from phones to depression even where studies of screen time alone find weak links.

text: Social media can harm teenagers through whole peer groups, so studies that measure only one teenager's own screen time understate the total effect of social media on teen mental health.
bottom_line: This is a reasonable objection to small individual-level correlations, but it is hard to test, and an argument that explains why the data look weak needs its own data before it can carry much weight.

text: When Facebook was introduced at a US college, students there reported feeling hopeless almost 0.1 standard deviations more often than students at colleges without Facebook, with worse readings the longer they were exposed.
bottom_line: A strong natural experiment showing social media can cause harm, but in college students on mid-2000s Facebook, and the effect size is modest.

text: Adults randomly paid to deactivate Facebook for four weeks before the 2018 US midterm election reported higher life satisfaction (0.12 standard deviations) and lower anxiety (0.10) and depression (0.09) than those who kept using it.
bottom_line: Clean causal evidence that social media use lowers mood somewhat, though the participants were adults and the effects are small.

text: Reanalyzing published social media reduction experiments, cutting or quitting social media for one week or longer improved mental health with a pooled effect of d = 0.156, while interventions shorter than a week showed a worse result (d = -0.175).
bottom_line: Suggests the null result in earlier pooled experiments came partly from mixing very short trials with longer ones, but the improvement it finds is still small and the trials are mostly not in teenagers.

text: Teen depression or self-harm measures in Australia will improve relative to New Zealand within three years of Australia's under-16 social media ban, among teens whose use actually fell.
Preregistered randomized trials of three weeks or longer that cut teenagers' social media use will show a pooled improvement of at least d = 0.2 on depression or anxiety scales.
A large randomized trial that removes social media from teenagers' phones for a full school term finds clinically meaningful drops in depression symptoms compared with a control group.
Within-country data show that regions where teenagers got smartphones and high-speed mobile internet earlier saw their rise in teen depression begin earlier.
The rise in teen depression and anxiety since 2012 is mostly a real increase in suffering, not mostly a change in how willing teenagers are to report symptoms.
Effects too small to see in one teenager's screen-time data can still add up to a large effect when whole peer groups move their social lives onto phones at once.
No other change that arrived around 2012, such as academic pressure or reduced independence, is large enough on its own to explain most of the rise in teen anxiety and depression.

Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt argues in his 2024 book The Anxious Generation that the shift to phone-based childhood in the early 2010s is the main cause of the rise in mental illness among teenagers.

Psychologist Jean Twenge argued in her September 2017 Atlantic article "Have Smartphones Destroyed a Generation?" that teenagers born after 1995 were on the brink of the worst mental health crisis in decades and tied that crisis to their smartphones.

U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy wrote in a June 17, 2024 New York Times op-ed that Congress should require a surgeon general's warning label on social media platforms stating that social media is associated with significant mental health harms for adolescents.
The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness, Jonathan Haidt, 2024
bridge: Haidt gathers the timing, sex-difference and cross-country trend data and argues that the move from play-based to phone-based childhood around 2010 to 2015 is the main cause of the rise in teen anxiety and depression.
bottom_line: It is the fullest statement of the case and worth reading as such, but it is an argument built from other people's studies, so its weight depends on those studies rather than on the book.

text: Social Media and Mental Health, Luca Braghieri, Ro'ee Levy and Alexey Makarin, 2022
bridge: Using the staggered rollout of Facebook across American colleges, the study finds that student mental health got worse where Facebook arrived compared with colleges where it had not yet arrived.
bottom_line: This deserves high weight as causal evidence because students did not choose the arrival dates, though it covers college students on early Facebook rather than teenagers on smartphones.

text: Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory, Office of the U.S. Surgeon General, 2023
where_found: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
bridge: The advisory concludes that there is not enough evidence to say social media is safe for children and adolescents and lists the risks of heavy use for youth mental health.
bottom_line: It carries public-health authority and signals official concern, but it argues for caution under uncertainty rather than showing that social media is the main cause.

text: Large studies of hundreds of thousands of teenagers find that time spent on digital technology explains well under one percent of the differences in teen well-being.
bottom_line: This weighs heavily against social media being the main cause, though critics answer that broad screen-time measures blur social media with harmless uses and so shrink the true effect.

text: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine reviewed the research in 2023 and concluded it did not support the claim that social media causes changes in adolescent health at the population level.
bottom_line: A consensus panel's judgment deserves real weight, but it reflects the evidence up to 2023, and 'not shown' is not the same as 'shown false'.

text: Other changes that hit American teenagers after 2008, such as heavier academic pressure, less unsupervised play, economic strain after the Great Recession and fear of school shootings, could explain much of the rise in teen anxiety and depression.
bottom_line: These rivals are plausible, but most of them lack a clean break around 2012, so they weaken the word 'main' more than they disprove a large role for social media.

text: Greater awareness of mental illness and less stigma since the early 2010s mean that part of the measured rise in teen depression reflects more teenagers naming and reporting symptoms rather than more teenagers having them.
bottom_line: This likely explains some of the survey rise, but it fits poorly with rises in hospital visits for self-harm and in suicide among young teenagers, which do not depend on how willing teens are to describe their feelings.

text: The link between heavy social media use and depression in teenagers may run the other way, because depressed teenagers withdraw from friends and spend more time alone online.
bottom_line: Reverse causation is real and shows up in long-term studies, which is why correlations alone cannot settle the question; it does not explain the results of natural experiments or quit-social-media trials.

text: Studies of well-being across 168 countries find no consistent worsening as internet and mobile broadband spread, which a single worldwide cause like smartphones would generally be expected to produce.
bottom_line: The scale is impressive, but the data cover all ages from 15 to 89 and broad well-being measures, so they can miss a harm concentrated in teenage girls.

text: Across three large datasets of adolescents in the US and UK, digital technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in adolescent well-being.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that broad screen time is a weak predictor of teen well-being, though it measures all digital use rather than social media specifically.

text: A preregistered meta-analysis of experiments asking people to cut or stop social media found an average effect of 0.088 on mental health, which was not statistically significant and was below the smallest effect the author set as meaningful.
bottom_line: Important because it pools the experimental evidence, but its choices about which studies to include and how to group them were disputed, and a 2025 reanalysis of the same studies reached a different result.

text: Comparing well-being and mental health measures with internet and mobile broadband adoption across 168 countries over 16 years found only small and inconsistent changes, not a consistent link between adoption and worse outcomes.
bottom_line: Large in scope but coarse, covering ages 15 to 89 at the country level, and a 2026 critique by Sigaud, Rausch, McClean and Haidt argues it cannot test effects on adolescents.

text: Australia's under-16 social media ban will show no relative improvement in teen depression or self-harm compared with New Zealand, even among teens whose social media use actually fell.

Teen depression rates in the United States will stay near their 2021 to 2023 levels even if teen time on social media drops by a quarter under new state laws, school phone bans and platform time limits.
Teen depression rates fall back toward 2011 levels in a country while teenagers' social media use there stays as high as ever.
Well-designed long-term studies find that depression predicts later social media use but social media use does not predict later depression once earlier symptoms are accounted for.
A cause strong enough to be the main driver of a national mental health trend should leave a clear signal in large studies of individual teenagers' technology use.
Teen mental health is shaped by many causes at once, so naming any single technology as the main cause oversimplifies how depression and anxiety develop.
Public alarm about a new medium for young people, as with television and video games before it, tends to run ahead of the evidence and should be discounted until experiments confirm it.

Psychologist Candice Odgers wrote in a March 2024 Nature review that the claim in The Anxious Generation that digital technologies are causing an epidemic of mental illness among young people is not supported by science.
The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use, Amy Orben and Andrew K. Przybylski, 2019
bridge: Running the same three large teen datasets through thousands of reasonable analysis choices, the study finds that digital technology use explains at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being.
bottom_line: It is a heavy blow to the idea that screen time is the main driver, though it measures broad digital use rather than social media specifically, which its critics say shrinks the effect.

text: Do social media experiments prove a link with mental health: A methodological and meta-analytic review, Christopher J. Ferguson, 2024
bridge: Pooling experiments in which people cut back on social media, the review finds an average effect on mental health that is statistically no different from zero, with large differences between studies.
bottom_line: It directly tests the strongest kind of evidence, but its choices about which studies and outcomes to pool have been publicly disputed by Haidt and Zach Rausch, so it narrows the case without closing it.

text: The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?, Candice L. Odgers, 2024
bridge: In this review of The Anxious Generation, Odgers writes that research consistently finds a mix of no, small and mixed associations between digital technology and teen mental health, and that the book's causal story is not supported by science.
bottom_line: It is a short review rather than new research, but it states the skeptical expert view clearly in a leading journal and points readers to the studies behind it.

text: Teenage girls need online spaces that do not push them into constant comparison of looks and popularity.
measured_by: Rates of depression, sadness and self-harm among teenage girls in national surveys such as the CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey.
if_true: Girls' depression and self-harm rates fall as appearance-focused feeds are limited or redesigned.
if_false: Girls' rates stay high after feeds change, and attention needs to move to other pressures on them.
bottom_line: Girls show the largest rise, so they have the most to gain if the belief is true and the most to lose if a wrong cause is pursued.

text: School teachers need classrooms where students' attention is not split by phones.
measured_by: Teacher reports of classroom distraction and student test scores in schools before and after phone bans.
if_true: Phone bans improve both attention in class and students' mood, giving teachers support for strict policies.
if_false: Phone bans may still help attention but will not ease the student mental health problems teachers see daily.
bottom_line: Teachers benefit from phone limits partly regardless of the answer, which makes their interest only partly tied to this belief.

text: LGBTQ teenagers in unsupportive towns need online communities where they can find people like them.
measured_by: Reported loneliness and depression among LGBTQ teenagers before and after social media restrictions.
if_true: Restrictions may still help most teens, but LGBTQ teens' loneliness could rise unless safe alternatives exist.
if_false: Restrictions take away a lifeline from LGBTQ teens without delivering the promised mental health gains.
bottom_line: A concrete group that social media often helps, so broad bans weigh especially heavily on them.

text: Child psychiatrists and school counselors need the other causes of teen depression, such as academic pressure, poverty and family stress, to get funding and attention.
measured_by: Public spending on youth mental health treatment and counselor-to-student ratios in schools.
if_true: Funding aimed at limiting social media is well spent, and treatment needs ease as rates fall.
if_false: Money and attention spent on phones leave the real drivers untreated and clinicians overwhelmed.
bottom_line: Their interest is not in defending social media but in making sure the response matches the actual causes.

text: Teenagers need to talk with friends online without handing their ID or face scans to tech companies.
measured_by: Share of teens and adults required to verify age, and reported data breaches involving age-verification records.
if_true: Some loss of privacy may be a fair price for large mental health gains.
if_false: Teens and adults give up privacy and freedom of speech online for no mental health benefit.
bottom_line: A cost that is easy to overlook because it falls on everyone in small amounts rather than on any one group heavily.

text: If social media is the main cause, delaying teen social media accounts until age 16 would lower the share of American 12-to-17-year-olds with a past-year major depressive episode.
bottom_line: A rough page estimate, assuming social media drove over half of the roughly 10-point rise since 2011 and that partial compliance recovers only part of that; it rests entirely on the belief being true.

text: Phone-free school days would give students more uninterrupted attention in class and more face-to-face time with classmates.
bottom_line: Likely to deliver some benefit to learning whether or not phones are the main cause of teen depression, which makes it a low-regret step.

text: Default overnight blocks on teen social media accounts would give teenagers more sleep on school nights.
bottom_line: Sleep loss is a well-supported risk for teen depression, so this benefit holds even under weaker versions of the belief, but no reliable estimate of the gain was found.

text: Age-verification rules for social media require teenagers and adults to give ID documents or face scans to platforms or third-party checkers.
bottom_line: A real privacy and access cost that falls on everyone, not just teens, and early Australian reports suggest many teens get around the checks anyway.

text: Cutting teenagers off from social media would remove support communities that isolated LGBTQ teenagers rely on.
bottom_line: A serious cost for a minority of teens, and one that grows if restrictions are broad rather than aimed at the most harmful features.

text: Treating phones as the main cause of teen depression could pull money and attention away from school counselors, clinics and other causes like academic pressure and family stress.
bottom_line: This cost is large only if the belief is false or overstated, which is exactly what is in dispute.

text: The change in teen depression and self-harm rates in a country that sharply cuts teen social media use, compared with similar countries that do not, is a fair measure of whether social media is the main cause of the rise in teen anxiety and depression.

The size of the mental health improvement in randomized trials that cut teenagers' social media use for three weeks or more is a fair measure of how much social media causes teen depression and anxiety.

Whether the rise in teen depression in each country begins when smartphone ownership among that country's teenagers passed one half, rather than in the same calendar year everywhere, is a fair measure of whether phones rather than some other shared event drove the rise.
Rates of anxiety and depression among American teenagers truly rose after about 2012, beyond what better diagnosis and reporting would produce.
Heavy smartphone and social media use causes worse mental health in teenagers, rather than only being more common among teenagers who are already struggling.
Smartphones and social media account for a larger share of the rise in teen anxiety and depression than any rival cause such as academic pressure, reduced independence or economic strain.
Schools that ban phones for the full school day would see fewer reports of distraction, bullying and peer conflict among students within the first year or two.
Teenagers who stop using social media for several weeks would report modest improvements in mood, sleep and anxiety within a year of cutting back.

If countries and states that restrict social media for children under 16 keep those limits for a decade, rates of teen depression and self-harm there would fall faster than in comparable places without the limits.
Over a decade, teenagers who grow up with later smartphone ownership would reach adulthood with lower rates of anxiety and depression than the cohort born in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Smartphones and social media are the sole cause of the rise in teenage anxiety and depression since 2012, and the rise would not have happened without them.
Smartphones and social media are so harmful to teenagers that children under 16 should be legally barred from using social media in every country.
Smartphones and social media are one of several significant causes of the rise in teenage anxiety and depression since 2012.
Heavy use of image-based social media harms the mental health of some teenage girls, even if it does not explain most of the national rise in teen depression.
Schools should ban phones during the school day.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that full-day phone bans sharply cut phone use in class and that teachers welcome them; it is thin and mixed on whether they raise test scores or improve mental health, with careful studies ranging from no effect to small gains after the first year and one large Norwegian finding on bullying and mental health. The real fight is whether less distraction is worth a first-year rise in suspensions and lost parent contact, and whether a class-time rule would get most of the benefit at less cost.
hook: In June 2023 fewer than one in four countries banned phones in schools; by March 2026, 114 education systems, 58% of countries, had a national ban, according to UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report.
question: Should schools ban students' phones for the whole school day, not just during class?
ask: This page most needs a study that follows students for three or more years after a full-day phone ban and measures test scores, mental health and discipline together.

text: Phones in class pull students' attention away from lessons, and most U.S. high school teachers call phone distraction a major classroom problem.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on the problem being real, since a Pew Research Center survey found 72% of high school teachers call it a major problem, but it says nothing yet about whether a full-day ban is the right fix.

text: A school-wide phone ban is easier for teachers to enforce than rules that leave each teacher to police phones lesson by lesson.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: Pew found 60% of high school teachers whose schools already had phone policies said those policies were hard to enforce, which points to clearer rules, though no study yet compares enforcement under the two designs directly.

text: Removing phones from middle schools reduces bullying among students, because much bullying now travels through phones during the school day.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight, resting mainly on one strong Norwegian study that found large drops in bullying after bans; it needs replication elsewhere.

text: When every student is without a phone, no single student pays a social price for logging off, so a school-wide ban solves a problem that individual self-control cannot.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the logic is sound and explains why bans are collective rules, but there is little direct measurement of the social pressure it describes.

text: Students from low-income families and low-achieving students gain the most when schools remove phone distractions, so school phone bans narrow achievement gaps.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: both the English study by Beland and Murphy and the Norwegian study by Abrahamsson found larger gains for these groups, but a Swedish study found no gains for anyone.

text: A school day without phones gives students several hours of face-to-face time with classmates, which builds social skills that screens tend to crowd out.
bottom_line: Light to moderate weight: school leaders in the Netherlands reported a better social climate after their ban, but that is a survey of leaders rather than a measure of students' skills.

text: In a large Florida urban school district with a bell-to-bell ban, test scores rose by about 1.1 percentiles in the second year after the ban, and unexcused absences fell.
bottom_line: Credible but small, and the authors estimate that better attendance explains about half the gain.

text: In a survey of 317 Dutch secondary school leaders after the Netherlands' 2024 classroom phone rule, 75% said students found it easier to concentrate and 59% reported a better social climate.
bottom_line: Light weight: these are school leaders' impressions, not measured student outcomes, and leaders who enforce a rule tend to report it works.

text: Follow-up studies of U.S. schools with full-day phone bans will find test score gains in the third or later year after adoption that are larger than the gains in the first year.
At least one study outside Norway will find that school phone bans reduce bullying or mental health visits among students, using records rather than one-time surveys.
A randomized trial in which some schools are assigned full-day phone bans finds clear gains in test scores and fewer mental health problems compared with schools that kept their old rules.
Several U.S. districts report that suspension rates returned to pre-ban levels within two years while unexcused absences stayed lower than before the ban.
Students' phone use during the school day harms learning or well-being enough that removing phones for the whole day produces gains worth the effort of enforcing a ban.
Schools have the rightful authority to restrict students' personal belongings, including phones, during school hours.
