A single school-wide phone rule works better than leaving phone limits to each teacher, each family or each student's self-control.
Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt argues in his 2024 book The Anxious Generation that schools should be phone-free from the first bell to the last, with phones locked away for the whole school day.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul pushed for and won a statewide bell-to-bell restriction on student smartphone use in New York schools in the 2025 state budget.

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the Phone-Free Schools Act (AB 3216) in September 2024, requiring every California school district to adopt a policy limiting or banning student smartphone use at school.
Ill Communication: Technology, distraction & student performance, Louis-Philippe Beland and Richard Murphy, 2016
bridge: Using English schools that introduced phone bans at different times, the study found test scores rose after bans, with the largest gains for low-achieving students.
bottom_line: Moderate to heavy weight: a careful and widely cited study, though it covers English schools in the 2000s, before nearly every student carried a smartphone.

text: Smartphone Bans, Student Outcomes and Mental Health, Sara Abrahamsson, 2026
where_found: Journal of Human Resources (earlier circulated as an SSRN preprint in 2024)
bridge: Studying Norwegian middle schools that banned smartphones at different times, the study found less bullying and fewer doctor visits for psychological symptoms among girls, with the biggest gains for girls from low-income families.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: a peer-reviewed study of the outcomes bans are meant to change, but from one country and needing replication in the United States.

text: The largest recent U.S. study of school phone bans found average effects on test scores close to zero, so full-day bans cost effort without a clear academic payoff.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the 2026 national pouch study by Allcott, Dee, Gentzkow and colleagues is the biggest and most careful evaluation so far, though it covers only the first few years and one kind of ban.

text: Parents need to be able to reach their children during emergencies such as lockdowns, and a full-day phone ban cuts that line of contact.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as a real parental need, but some school safety experts argue phones in a lockdown can distract students or slow an evacuation, so the safety effect cuts both ways.

text: Enforcing a new school phone ban increases suspensions, which takes students out of class and falls hardest on Black students.
bottom_line: Heavy weight for the first year, since two separate U.S. studies found suspensions rose after bans, but both also found the increase faded within a year or two.

text: A ban on phones during the school day does not lower teenagers' total screen time or social media use, so it cannot fix the mental health harms blamed on phones.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the UK SMART Schools study found students at restrictive schools used phones and social media about as much overall, but it was a one-time comparison and cannot show cause.

text: Students who never practice managing a phone at school miss the chance to learn the self-control they will need as adults.
bottom_line: Light weight: the argument is plausible, but no study shows that phone access at school builds self-control, and adults also learn self-control in places with rules.

text: A rule that bans phones only during class stops lesson-time distraction while leaving lunch and breaks alone, so a full-day ban goes further than the problem requires.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: most of the measured harm is in-class distraction, but the Norwegian bullying results suggest that breaks and lunch matter too.

text: Among 1,227 students aged 12 to 15 at 30 English schools, students at schools with restrictive phone policies showed no better mental wellbeing and no lower total phone or social media use than students at permissive schools.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a careful snapshot, but a one-time comparison of schools cannot show what a ban causes over time.

text: In the first month of a Florida district's bell-to-bell phone ban, suspensions rose 25% over the prior year, and in-school suspensions of Black students at high-use schools rose about 30%.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on a real short-term cost, matched by the national pouch study's suspension rise, though both found it faded after the first year.

text: Follow-up studies of U.S. full-day phone bans will find average test score effects that remain within about one percentile of zero three or more years after adoption.
Studies comparing U.S. states with and without full-day school phone bans will find no larger drop in teenagers' reported persistent sadness or hopelessness in the ban states.
Multi-year data from U.S. states with bell-to-bell bans show no test score gains and no mental health improvement after the first two years.
A study finds that students at schools with full-day phone bans spend more total time on social media after school, wiping out any time saved during the school day.
Parents need direct, instant contact with their children during the school day, and calls through the school office are not an adequate substitute in an emergency.
Teaching students to manage phones responsibly produces better long-term habits than removing phones from the school day.
A school rule that adds discipline and enforcement costs should show measurable gains in learning or well-being before it is imposed on every student.

New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio lifted the city's longstanding ban on cell phones in public schools in 2015, saying parents needed to be able to stay in touch with their children, especially in an emergency.

Victoria Goodyear of the University of Birmingham, lead author of the 2025 SMART Schools study, reported that its results do not provide evidence to support restrictive school phone policies as a way to improve teenagers' mental wellbeing or cut their overall phone use.
The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches, Hunt Allcott, E. Jason Baron, Thomas Dee, Angela Duckworth, Matthew Gentzkow and Brian Jacob, 2026
where_found: National Bureau of Economic Research Working Paper
bridge: Pouch bans sharply cut phone use, but average effects on test scores were close to zero, disciplinary incidents rose in the first year, and the authors found no clear gain in classroom attention or perceived online bullying.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: the largest U.S. evaluation so far, though it is not yet peer reviewed, covers only pouch bans, and found well-being turning positive in later years.

text: School phone policies and their association with mental wellbeing, phone use, and social media use (SMART Schools): a cross-sectional observational study, Victoria A. Goodyear and colleagues, 2025
bridge: Comparing English secondary schools with restrictive and permissive phone rules, the study found no evidence that restrictive rules went with better mental wellbeing or less overall phone and social media use.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a peer-reviewed study of the right outcomes, but a one-time snapshot that cannot show cause and effect.

text: The impact of banning mobile phones in Swedish secondary schools, Dany Kessel, Hulda Lif Hardardottir and Björn Tyrefors, 2020
bridge: Swedish schools that banned phones saw no measurable change in student test scores compared with schools that did not.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: a peer-reviewed null result that tempers the English and Norwegian findings, though Swedish ban rules varied in how strictly they were enforced.

text: High school teachers need classrooms where students are not pulled away from lessons by their phones.
measured_by: The share of teachers who call phone distraction a major classroom problem, as surveyed by Pew Research Center, and the share of students seen using phones in class.
if_true: Both shares fall sharply in schools with full-day bans.
if_false: The shares fall little or come back as students find ways around the ban.
bottom_line: The best-served interest: bans reliably cut in-class phone use, according to the national pouch study.

text: Middle school girls need a school day free of online bullying and constant social comparison.
measured_by: Reported bullying rates and visits to doctors for psychological symptoms among middle school girls.
if_true: Both fall after a ban, as they did in Norway.
if_false: Neither changes, or the bullying simply moves to after school.
bottom_line: Strongly supported by one Norwegian study and contradicted by a UK snapshot, so the measure is still open.

text: Students from low-income families need school hours that protect their focus, since they gain the most when distractions are removed.
measured_by: Test score and grade gaps between low-income and higher-income students before and after a ban.
if_true: The gap narrows after a ban.
if_false: The gap stays the same, or low-income students lose class time to suspensions.
bottom_line: Supported by English and Norwegian findings, but no U.S. study has yet confirmed it.

text: Parents need to reach their children quickly in an emergency such as a school lockdown.
measured_by: The time it takes parents to confirm their child is safe during a school emergency, and parents' reported confidence in school communication systems.
if_true: Schools with bans build fast alert systems and parents' confidence recovers.
if_false: Parents are cut off during emergencies and lose trust in the school.
bottom_line: A widely held and sincere need; a National Parents Union poll found 78% of parents whose children take phones to school cite emergencies as the reason.

text: Black students need school rules that do not push them out of class through uneven discipline.
measured_by: Suspension rates by race before and after a phone ban.
if_true: Any rise in suspensions fades within a year, with no lasting racial gap.
if_false: Suspensions of Black students stay elevated and the racial gap widens.
bottom_line: Backed by the Florida study's 30% rise in in-school suspensions of Black students at high-use schools in the first year.

text: Students with diabetes, disabilities or limited English need their phones for glucose monitors, translation apps and other supports.
measured_by: Whether students with documented needs receive exemptions promptly and keep using their supports during the school day.
if_true: Exemptions work and these students keep their supports.
if_false: Students go without needed supports while exemptions are processed or denied.
bottom_line: A real need that most bans address on paper, so the question is how well schools carry out the exemptions.

text: A full-day school phone ban cuts the share of students using phones in class for personal reasons by roughly 48 percentage points.
bottom_line: The best-established benefit on the page, from the national pouch study's teacher survey (61% down to 13%).

text: A full-day school phone ban raises middle and high school students' test scores by about one percentile once the first year has passed.
bottom_line: Small and not yet replicated nationally; the Florida study found it, the national pouch study found near-zero averages.

text: A middle school smartphone ban reduces bullying among girls.
bottom_line: A large effect from one Norwegian study; until it is replicated it should be treated as promising rather than settled.

text: Enforcing a new school phone ban raises suspension rates in its first year.
bottom_line: Found in two separate U.S. studies (16% nationally, 25% in one Florida district's first month), and both found it faded after a year.

text: A full-day phone ban delays parents' contact with their children during a school lockdown or other emergency.
bottom_line: A real worry for many parents, but no study measures the delay or whether phone contact during a lockdown helps or harms.

text: A full-day phone ban can cut students with disabilities or medical conditions off from phone-based supports when exemptions are slow or poorly run.
bottom_line: Most bans written into law include medical and disability exemptions, so the cost depends on how well schools carry them out.

text: The change in standardized test scores two or more years after a school adopts a full-day phone ban, compared with similar schools that did not, is a fair measure of whether the ban helps students learn.

The rate of mental health visits and reported bullying among students at ban schools, compared with similar students at non-ban schools, is a fair measure of whether school phone bans protect students' wellbeing.
Suspension rates in the two years after a phone ban, broken out by student race, are a fair measure of the discipline cost of school phone bans.
Students' use of phones during the school day measurably harms their learning, behavior or well-being.
A ban on phones for the whole school day reduces students' harmful phone use more than a class-time-only rule or a teacher-by-teacher rule does.
The gains from a full-day school phone ban outweigh its costs, including added suspensions and less direct contact between parents and children.
Within the first school year of a full-day phone ban, teachers report students using phones in class far less often than before the ban.
Within the first school year of a full-day phone ban, disciplinary incidents and suspensions rise as students and staff adjust to the new rule, then begin to fall in the second year.
Schools should require students to leave their phones at home and ban phones from school grounds entirely.
Governments should require every public school to ban student phones for the whole school day, with no local opt-out.
Schools should ban phone use during class time but allow students to use phones at lunch and between classes.
Each school should choose its own phone policy, with a full-day ban as one option among several.
TikTok has done more harm than good to the people who use it.
bottom_line: The evidence is strong that TikTok is designed to maximize watching and that many users, by their own paid choices, would rather it did not exist; it is thin and mostly correlational on whether TikTok causes lasting harm to the typical user's mind or mood. The real fight is over whether the hours people choose to spend on TikTok prove it is good for them, or show a habit they cannot escape alone.
hook: When TikTok tested a 60-minute time-limit prompt for teens, average use fell only from about 108.5 to 107 minutes a day, and a project manager wrote in internal documents, "Our goal is not to reduce the time spent" (NPR and Kentucky Public Radio, October 2024).
question: Has TikTok, on balance, done more harm than good to the people who use it?
ask: Point us to, or help run, a randomized trial that pays people to quit TikTok specifically for several weeks and measures their mood, sleep and attention against people who kept using it.

text: TikTok's endless, autoplaying feed is built to keep people watching longer than they mean to, and TikTok's own internal test found that its time-limit tool cut teen viewing by only about a minute and a half a day.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: it rests on the company's own documents rather than outside critics, though it shows the design aim and not by itself the harm.

text: Many active TikTok users would be better off if TikTok did not exist for anyone, which means that their continued use reflects a social trap rather than proof that TikTok benefits them.
bottom_line: Heavy weight because it is measured with real money rather than opinion, but so far it rests on one study of U.S. college students.

text: TikTok's recommendation algorithm can steer new teenage accounts toward suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder videos within minutes of joining.
bottom_line: Serious for the vulnerable minority it reaches, but audits use a handful of test accounts, so they show what can happen more than how often it does.

text: Frequent watching of short TikTok-style videos goes along with weaker attention and self-control in people of all ages.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the pattern holds across dozens of studies, but nearly all of them are correlations that cannot show which comes first.

text: For heavy TikTok users, hours on the app crowd out sleep, schoolwork and time with friends and family, as TikTok's own researchers acknowledged.
bottom_line: Real for heavy users, who are a large minority of teens, but weaker as a claim about the typical user who watches in short breaks.

text: In an incentivized experiment with more than 1,000 U.S. college students, active TikTok users demanded about $59 on average to deactivate TikTok for four weeks on their own, yet would pay about $28 to have everyone, themselves included, deactivate it, and almost two-thirds of active users appeared to lose welfare from TikTok existing.
bottom_line: The most direct test of the belief yet run, but it is one study of college students, and the published version reports somewhat different dollar figures from the working paper.

text: TikTok's internal test of a 60-minute daily time-limit prompt found that it cut average teen use only from about 108.5 to about 107 minutes a day, and internal documents said a user can form a habit after watching 260 videos.
bottom_line: Strong evidence about TikTok's design and intent because it is the company's own data, though the figures come from excerpts selected for a lawsuit.

text: Test accounts posing as 13-year-olds were shown suicide content within 2.6 minutes and eating-disorder content within 8 minutes, and accounts flagged as vulnerable got 12 times more self-harm and suicide recommendations than standard accounts.
bottom_line: Shows the feed can push harmful material fast, but it used a small number of accounts in 2022 from an advocacy group, and TikTok has changed its systems since.

text: A randomized trial in which TikTok users are paid to quit TikTok for at least four weeks will find that those who quit report better mood or sleep than those who kept using it.

A replication of the collective-deactivation experiment with a sample that is not limited to college students will find that most active TikTok users would pay to have TikTok switched off for everyone.
A randomized trial finds that people paid to stop using TikTok for a month sleep more and report higher life satisfaction than people who kept using it.
Internal TikTok research released in court shows that the company measured worse well-being among its heavier users and found that heavier use came first.
Time spent watching TikTok is mostly taken from sleep, schoolwork and time with people rather than from other screens or other idle pastimes.
What TikTok users would give up to have TikTok gone for everyone is a better measure of TikTok's value to them than the fact that they keep opening the app.
Serious harm to a vulnerable minority of TikTok users, such as teenagers steered toward self-harm videos, can outweigh the ordinary enjoyment TikTok gives a much larger number of casual users.
Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, writing with Zach Rausch on After Babel in January 2025, argued that TikTok harms children at an industrial scale and should be removed from American childhood.

New York Attorney General Letitia James co-led a bipartisan group of state attorneys general that sued TikTok in October 2024, alleging that TikTok's addictive design harms young users' mental health.
Deadly by Design, Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2022
where_found: Center for Countering Digital Hate (counterhate.com), published December 15, 2022
bridge: New TikTok accounts set up as 13-year-olds in four countries were shown suicide content within 2.6 minutes and eating-disorder content within 8 minutes, and accounts with names suggesting weight worries got far more self-harm videos.
bottom_line: Strong evidence of what TikTok's feed can do to a vulnerable teenager, but it rests on a small number of test accounts, so it shows risk more than how common the harm is.

text: When Product Markets Become Collective Traps: The Case of Social Media, Leonardo Bursztyn, Benjamin Handel, Rafael Jimenez-Duran and Christopher Roth, 2025
where_found: American Economic Review, vol. 115, no. 12 (December 2025); earlier as NBER Working Paper 31771 (2023)
bridge: Paid experiments with U.S. college students found that TikTok shows a positive value when only users are counted but a negative value once the cost to people left out is counted, and that many active users would prefer TikTok not exist at all.
bottom_line: Heavy weight because it uses real money rather than opinion and passed peer review at a top journal, though it studies college students rather than all users.

text: Most people use TikTok for entertainment, and enjoying funny, beautiful or interesting videos is a real good, not a harm.
bottom_line: Strong weight because people do value it, as shown by what users demand to give it up; whether that value outweighs the harms is the open question.

text: TikTok lets small businesses and independent creators reach large audiences cheaply, and that reach has produced real sales and income.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: the business gains are real, but the largest dollar estimates come from a study TikTok paid for, and these gains go to sellers more than to ordinary viewers.

text: Most teenagers say social media makes them feel more connected to their friends, and only a small share say social media hurts them personally.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it is what users themselves report, but it covers social media in general rather than TikTok alone, and people can misjudge habits they enjoy.

text: TikTok gives adults under 30 a free, fast source of news and practical how-to information that older media were not reaching them with.
bottom_line: Some weight: the reach is measured and large, but the quality of that news varies and TikTok's own feed decides what people see.

text: 74% of U.S. teens said social media makes them feel more connected to their friends and 63% said it gives them a place to show their creative side, while only 14% said social media hurts them personally, even though 48% said it mostly hurts people their age.
bottom_line: A large representative survey of users' own judgment, but it covers social media generally, and the gap between 'it hurts others' and 'it hurts me' cuts both ways.

text: A randomized trial in which TikTok users are paid to quit TikTok for at least four weeks will find no meaningful improvement in mood, sleep or attention among those who quit.
Long-term studies that follow teenagers for a year or more will find that heavier TikTok use does not predict later depression or anxiety once earlier symptoms are accounted for.
A nationally representative replication finds that most active TikTok users would not pay anything to have TikTok disappear for everyone.
A long-term study of teenagers finds that heavier TikTok use does not predict later depression, anxiety or poorer sleep once earlier symptoms are taken into account.
Adults and teenagers who keep choosing to use TikTok are generally the best judges of whether TikTok is good for them.
If TikTok vanished, most of its users would move to rival short-video feeds such as YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, so TikTok's own share of any harm is small.
The link between heavy TikTok use and poor mental health mostly reflects struggling people seeking out TikTok rather than TikTok making people struggle.
Social Media and Adolescent Health, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024
bridge: A national expert committee reviewed the research and concluded that it does not support the claim that social media causes changes in adolescent health across the whole population, while finding both benefits and risks for particular young people.
bottom_line: Heavy weight as the most careful neutral review available, though it covers social media in general rather than TikTok alone and predates the newest TikTok studies.

text: Teens, Social Media and Mental Health, Michelle Faverio, Monica Anderson and Eugenie Park, 2025
bridge: In a national survey, 74% of U.S. teens said social media makes them feel more connected to their friends and only 14% said it hurts them personally, though 48% said it mostly hurts people their age.
bottom_line: Moderate weight as a large, careful survey of what teenagers themselves report, but it does not separate TikTok from other apps, and the gap between 14% and 48% shows people may misjudge their own habits.

text: Parents of teenagers need their children's apps to stop steering them toward self-harm and eating-disorder videos.
measured_by: The share of fresh teen test accounts shown suicide, self-harm or eating-disorder videos in their first 30 minutes in independent audits.
if_true: The share stays high, as in the 2022 audit, and falls only under outside pressure.
if_false: The share is low or near zero in repeated audits.
bottom_line: A strong interest for a minority of families whose children are vulnerable, and one that parents cannot meet by watching over their children's shoulders.

text: College students need a way out of apps they keep using but wish nobody used.
measured_by: The share of student users who would pay to have TikTok switched off for everyone in incentivized experiments.
if_true: Most active users would pay to have everyone deactivate, as in the 2023 experiment.
if_false: Few active users would pay anything to have everyone deactivate.
bottom_line: The interest the best evidence speaks to most directly, though measured so far in one group of students.

text: Small-business owners need a cheap way to reach new customers.
measured_by: Sales that independent surveys of businesses attribute to TikTok, compared with sales through other advertising channels.
if_true: Businesses could replace TikTok sales through other channels at little extra cost.
if_false: Businesses that lose TikTok lose sales they cannot replace elsewhere.
bottom_line: A real interest, though it concerns sellers' income more than whether watching TikTok is good for viewers.

text: Independent creators and authors need a way to find an audience without a publisher or studio choosing for them.
measured_by: Print sales that Circana BookScan ties to BookTok, and creator income reported on the platform.
if_true: BookTok-tied sales and creator income would be matched by other platforms if TikTok shrank.
if_false: BookTok-tied sales keep growing and have no equal on other platforms.
bottom_line: Backed by independent sales data, and a benefit that reaches readers as well as authors.

text: If TikTok users left the app together, college-student users would gain about as much as the $28 a month each that they said they would pay to have everyone deactivate it.
bottom_line: The only measured figure for the gain, but it comes from one college sample and assumes everyone leaves at once.

text: Teenagers who cut TikTok back from the roughly 108 minutes a day seen in TikTok's own test to one hour would regain about 48 minutes a day for sleep, schoolwork and people.
bottom_line: A simple subtraction from TikTok's own figure, which assumes the freed time goes to better uses rather than to another app.

text: Changing how TikTok recommends videos to young accounts would cut the number of vulnerable teenagers who are shown suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder videos.
bottom_line: Likely real but not yet measurable, because no current audit gives a reliable baseline share.

text: Restricting or abandoning TikTok would cost small and medium-sized U.S. businesses a share of the sales tied to their TikTok use, which TikTok's commissioned study put at $24.2 billion of GDP in 2023.
bottom_line: An upper bound from a study TikTok paid for, since many of those sales would move to other platforms.

text: Restricting or abandoning TikTok would cut the book sales that Circana tied to BookTok, about 59 million U.S. print books in 2024.
bottom_line: Independent data, but some of those readers would find books another way, so the true loss is smaller.

text: Users who gave up TikTok while others kept using it would lose entertainment and connection that college-student users valued at about $59 a month each.
bottom_line: A real loss as users measure it, though part of that price reflects fear of missing out rather than enjoyment.

text: The share of active TikTok users in a nationally representative sample who would pay to have TikTok switched off for everyone is a fair measure of whether users themselves judge TikTok a net harm.
The difference in well-being, sleep and attention scores after four weeks off TikTok, in a randomized deactivation trial, is a fair measure of whether TikTok use harms the people who use it.

The share of fresh teen test accounts that are shown suicide, self-harm or eating-disorder videos within their first 30 minutes, in independent audits, is a fair measure of how much TikTok's feed exposes young users to harmful content.
Heavy TikTok use causes worse sleep, attention or mood in the people who use it, rather than merely going along with those problems.
The harm TikTok does to its users is larger than the enjoyment, information, connection and income it gives them, when both are counted in a common measure.
Whether TikTok is good for its users should be judged by their well-being over months and years rather than by their moment-to-moment choices to keep watching.
If families and lawmakers act on the belief that TikTok harms its users, more U.S. states will require default time limits, age checks or nighttime shutoffs for minors on TikTok within a year or two.

Teenagers who cut back on TikTok because of these limits will sleep more on school nights within months, while creators and small sellers who depend on TikTok will lose some income as their audiences shrink.

Over a decade, rules aimed at TikTok's design will spread to rival short-video feeds on YouTube and Instagram, because the same autoplaying feed would otherwise carry the same harm to a different app.

Over a decade, teenagers who grow up with limits on short-video apps will report better sleep and attention and lower rates of self-harm than teenagers did in the early 2020s, if TikTok was in fact a cause of those problems.
TikTok has done more harm than good even to the adults who use TikTok casually for a few minutes a day.
Every short-video feed built like TikTok's, including YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, does more harm than good to anyone who uses it.
TikTok has done more harm than good to teenagers who use TikTok for several hours a day.
TikTok's recommendation feed does some avoidable harm to vulnerable teenage users, even if most TikTok users come out ahead.
Images made by AI from a text prompt are art.
bottom_line: The evidence is solid that people often cannot tell the best prompt-made images from celebrated human art in blind tests, and equally solid that the same image is rated lower once it is labeled AI-made. What is thin is any measure of how much of a finished image the person who typed the prompt actually controls, and that is the real fight: whether art is judged by the object and the choices behind its selection, or by a human making the expressive choices themselves.
hook: In 2022 a picture Jason Allen made in Midjourney took first place for digital art at the Colorado State Fair, and in 2023 the U.S. Copyright Office refused to register it even though Allen had entered at least 624 prompts and revisions to make it.
question: Are images made by AI from a text prompt art?
ask: The page most needs a controlled study measuring how closely skilled prompters can make an image match an intention they wrote down before they started.

text: A person who writes, revises and selects among hundreds of text-to-image outputs is making creative choices of the same kind a photographer makes when choosing a subject, a framing and one frame from many.
bottom_line: Strong if the person really does iterate and select, since selection is already accepted as authorship in photography and collage; weak for a single unedited prompt.

text: Viewers in blind tests generally cannot tell good prompt-made images from celebrated human-made art and often like the prompt-made ones as much, so the difference people claim is mostly outside the image itself.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it shows prompt-made images can do what art does for a viewer, but not that a viewer's response is the whole definition of art.

text: Photography was first dismissed by many critics as mechanical copying rather than art and is now hung in every major museum, so text-to-image tools are likely to follow the same path.
bottom_line: A fair analogy that shows the objection has been wrong before, but an analogy is not proof, and a camera leaves far more of the visible detail to the person than a text-to-image model does.

text: Text-to-image tools let people who never learned to draw or paint turn a visual idea they hold into a finished picture, which widens who gets to make art.
bottom_line: Matters for whether prompt-made work is good for culture, though it bears more on its value than on whether the output is art.

text: A person who prompts toward a picture they have in mind is expressing an intention, and intention to express or communicate is what most definitions of art require.
bottom_line: Strong where the intention is real and specific; weaker to the degree the model, not the person, decides most of what the finished image shows.

text: In a study of more than 4 million artworks by more than 50,000 users, artists who adopted text-to-image AI produced 25 percent more work and saw the chance of a favorite per view rise by 50 percent over time.
bottom_line: Good evidence that peers value prompt-assisted work, though favorites on one art-sharing platform are a narrow measure, and the same study found average visual novelty declined.

text: About 11,000 people asked to sort fifty pictures into human art and AI images had a median accuracy of 60 percent, only a little above chance, and the two best-liked pictures of the fifty were both made by AI.
bottom_line: Large but self-selected sample with hand-picked images on both sides, so it shows the best prompt-made images can pass, not that typical ones do.

text: At least one of the Museum of Modern Art, Tate, the Centre Pompidou or the Whitney Museum will add to its permanent collection a work made mainly by text prompting an image generator.

A new random-label experiment on a representative U.S. sample will find the rating gap between human-labeled and AI-labeled versions of the same image smaller than the gaps Bellaiche and colleagues reported in 2023.
A controlled study finds that skilled prompters can make images that independent judges match to the prompters' own pre-written intentions as reliably as images made by hand illustrators.
Repeated experiments find that the rating penalty for an AI label disappears among people who are familiar with how text-to-image tools are used.
Whether an image is art depends on the human intention and choices behind it, not on whose hand or which machine made the marks.
Writing, revising and choosing among many machine-made images is a form of authorship, much as choosing one frame from many is for a photographer.
The response of viewers who find an image moving or meaningful counts toward whether that image is art.

German artist Boris Eldagsen, who turned down a 2023 Sony World Photography Award for an image he made with an AI image generator, said AI images are not photographs but described making them as a co-creation in which he is the director and named the practice promptography.
Can Computers Create Art?, Aaron Hertzmann, 2018
where_found: Arts (MDPI), special issue Machine as Artist (21st Century)
bridge: Hertzmann argues that art is made by social agents, so a computer cannot be credited as the artist, which places authorship of machine-assisted images with the person who uses the tool rather than ruling the images out as art.
bottom_line: A careful scholarly case that the tool is not the artist, useful to supporters only if one accepts that the person prompting is acting as the artist; it predates today's text-to-image models.

text: A text prompt describes an idea while the image model decides nearly every visible detail of the picture, so most of the expressive choices in a prompt-made image are not made by the person who typed the prompt.
bottom_line: The strongest objection, and the one the U.S. Copyright Office adopted in 2025; it weakens as people add editing, inpainting and hand work on top of the output.

text: Art is a form of communication between minds, and an image model has no intention, so the marks it produces mean nothing beyond what a viewer reads into them.
bottom_line: Persuasive to many, as Ted Chiang argued in The New Yorker in 2024, but it leaves room for the prompting person's own intention to supply the meaning.

text: Describing a picture to someone else who then makes it is commissioning rather than making, so a person who describes an image to an image model is closer to a patron than to an artist.
bottom_line: A sharp distinction that fits the single-prompt case well; it fits less well when the person iterates hundreds of times and edits the result.

text: Making a prompt-made image takes seconds and needs no skill built through years of practice, and skill and effort are part of what people value when they call something art.
bottom_line: Matches how many people feel, as labeled-art experiments show, but conceptual art already separates art from manual skill, so this argues for lower value more than for no art at all.

text: Across four experiments with 1,708 participants, the same artwork was liked less when labeled AI-made because it was seen as less creative and stirred less awe, and the effect was stronger in people who believe creativity is uniquely human.
bottom_line: Confirms the label penalty, but its authors read it as a bias protecting a worldview, which cuts partly for the belief.

text: Most of the ten largest U.S. state fairs will bar AI-generated images from their fine arts competitions or confine them to a separate AI category.
A federal court will rule in Allen v. Perlmutter that Jason Allen's prompts did not make him the author of the Midjourney-generated parts of Théâtre D'opéra Spatial.
A study finds that different people given the same brief produce text-to-image results that judges cannot tell apart, showing the person adds little beyond the model's defaults.
Repeated experiments find that people who make prompt-made images themselves still rate the same image lower when it is labeled AI-made.
A work is art only if the person credited with it made most of the specific expressive choices that a viewer can see in it.
An image model has no intentions of its own, so the details it fills in carry no meaning from any mind.
Describing a picture for someone or something else to make is commissioning it, and commissioning a picture does not make a person an artist.

Science fiction writer Ted Chiang argued in The New Yorker in 2024 that text-to-image generators are not going to make art, because a person typing a short prompt makes only a handful of the many choices that art requires.
Why A.I. Isn't Going to Make Art, Ted Chiang, 2024
bridge: Chiang argues that art is the product of many choices made by the artist, and that a short text prompt supplies only a few choices while the image model fills in the rest by averaging over its training data.
bottom_line: The most widely read case against, strong on the single short prompt, weaker for people who iterate, edit and select at length.

text: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability, U.S. Copyright Office, 2025
bridge: The report concludes that prompts alone do not give a user enough control over an AI system's output to make the user its author, while human selection, arrangement and modification of the output can still be protected.
bottom_line: Weighty as the official U.S. position on authorship, but it answers a legal question about copyright, not the broader question of whether the image is art.

text: Hobbyists without drawing training need tools that let them turn a visual idea into a finished picture.
measured_by: Number of people who make and share finished visual work each year
if_true: Rises as text-prompted work is accepted and shown alongside other art.
if_false: Stays limited to people with years of hand training.
bottom_line: A large and real group whose gain does not depend on the work being called art, only on it being allowed.

text: People with physical disabilities that limit hand control need ways to make pictures without holding a brush or stylus.
measured_by: Share of disabled artists who say they can make the images they intend
if_true: Rises as prompt-based tools count as a legitimate art practice.
if_false: Stays where it is, with their prompt-made work dismissed as not real art.
bottom_line: A small group with a strong claim, though no survey yet measures the effect.

text: Designers who work with AI image tools need their work judged and credited on the same terms as other art.
measured_by: Share of competitions, galleries and copyright offices that accept their work on ordinary terms
if_true: Rises toward full acceptance.
if_false: Falls as separate categories, bans and copyright refusals spread.
bottom_line: Their claim rests on how much of the image they actually control, which is the open question.

text: Painters and illustrators who enter juried competitions need categories where they are not judged against machine output.
measured_by: Share of major competitions with separate rules for AI-made entries
if_true: Falls as prompt-made work enters ordinary categories.
if_false: Rises as competitions separate or bar AI-made entries.
bottom_line: A practical need that can be met by separate categories without settling whether the work is art.

text: Artists who adopt text-to-image tools produce more finished works in the same time than they did before.
bottom_line: Taken from Zhou and Lee's 2024 study of one platform, so it is a real figure for that setting and an uncertain one elsewhere.

text: Treating text-prompted images as art gives people whose disabilities limit hand control a recognized way to make and show visual work.
bottom_line: Plausible and important, but no study counts how many people it reaches.

text: Accepting text-prompted images as art speeds the loss of paid commissions for working illustrators.
bottom_line: From a 2024 Society of Authors survey of its UK members, which is self-reported and not a representative sample.

text: Accepting text-prompted images as art lowers what illustrators can charge for the work they still get.
bottom_line: Same 2024 Society of Authors survey, so the same limits apply.

text: Accepting text-prompted images as art makes it harder for buyers to know how much of a piece a human actually made.
bottom_line: A real risk that grows as detection gets harder, but no one has measured it.

text: Accepting text-prompted images as art puts hand-made entries in juried competitions up against images that took far less time to make.
bottom_line: The Colorado State Fair and Sony World Photography Awards cases show it happens; how often is not counted.

text: The rate at which independent judges can match a prompt-made image to a written description of the intended picture that its maker recorded before starting is a fair measure of how much the person, rather than the model, decides what the image shows.
The gap in ratings between the same image labeled human-made and labeled AI-made is a fair measure of whether the objection to prompt-made images is about the work or about its label.

The share of major juried art competitions and museum collections that accept text-prompted images on the same terms as other digital art is a fair measure of whether the art world treats prompt-made images as art.
A person who writes a text prompt for an image model makes creative choices that meaningfully shape what the finished image looks like.
Art can be made through a tool that decides most visible details on its own, as long as a person directs the tool and chooses the result.
Being art does not require hand skill built through years of practice.
If images made by AI from text prompts are accepted as art, more art competitions will add separate categories for them instead of banning them outright.
If images made by AI from text prompts are accepted as art, more people without drawing training will publicly show and sell prompt-made images as their own artwork.
If images made by AI from text prompts are accepted as art, art schools will teach prompting, iterating and selecting among model outputs as a studio practice alongside drawing and photography.
If images made by AI from text prompts are accepted as art, major museums will collect and exhibit them as a recognized medium, the way they came to collect photography.
Every image an AI model produces from a text prompt is art, however little thought or effort went into the prompt.
The person who writes the text prompt is the sole author of an AI-generated image and deserves full copyright in it.
Images made by AI from text prompts can be art when the person iterates many times, selects carefully and edits the result.
Images made by AI from text prompts deserve to be judged in art competitions, in categories of their own.
AI-written novels will outsell human-written novels within ten years.
bottom_line: Strong evidence shows AI can write short passages that readers enjoy and often cannot tell from human work, and can do it cheaply; there is no evidence yet that AI-written novels win large sales, and outselling means taking more than half of all novel sales. The real fight is over whether readers buy authors or stories, whether AI labels become visible, and whether heavily edited hybrid books count as AI-written at all.
hook: For a median cost of $81 per author, researchers fine-tuned ChatGPT on award-winning novelists' books, and both general and MFA-trained readers preferred its imitations over those written by trained human writers (Chakrabarty, Ginsburg and Dhillon, 2025).
question: Will novels written mainly by AI sell more copies than novels written by people by October 2036?
ask: This page most needs a real sales figure for novels disclosed as AI-generated, from Amazon's KDP disclosures, Circana BookScan or a publisher report.

text: Large language models can already write fiction passages that ordinary readers, in blind tests, rate as highly as or higher than passages by professional human writers.
bottom_line: Strong weight on whether AI prose can please readers, but the tests so far use poems and short excerpts, not 300-page novels.

text: AI-written novels cost a tiny fraction of what human-written novels cost to produce, so publishers can sell them more cheaply and release far more of them.
bottom_line: Heavy weight, since price and volume drive genre sales, though cheap production has not yet been shown to produce matching sales.

text: Readers of fast-release genre series, such as romance and fantasy, reward familiar tropes and frequent new installments, which AI can supply faster than any human author.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it names the market where AI novels are most likely to win first, but genre readers are also among the most loyal to named authors.

text: Most readers cannot reliably tell whether a novel was written by a person or by an AI, so a stated preference for human authors will rarely change what they actually buy.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: detection studies support it, but it fails wherever books are clearly labeled.

text: No U.S. law requires a bookseller to tell buyers that a novel's text was generated by AI, so AI-written novels can compete on the same digital shelves as human-written ones.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it lowers the barrier today, but retailers or lawmakers could add labels well within ten years.

text: AI writing has improved so fast in the last five years that judging its ten-year prospects by today's weaknesses is likely to underestimate it.
bottom_line: Some weight as a trend argument, but past speed of improvement does not guarantee future speed, and sales depend on readers, not only on quality.

text: In two experiments with 1,634 and 696 participants, non-expert readers identified poems written by ChatGPT 3.5 with 46.6 percent accuracy, below chance, and rated the AI poems more favorably than poems by well-known human poets on most qualities, including rhythm and beauty.
bottom_line: Solid evidence that ordinary readers enjoy AI writing in blind conditions, but it concerns short poems, not novels people pay for.

text: When ChatGPT was fine-tuned on the complete works of 50 award-winning authors, 516 general readers preferred its imitations over those of MFA-trained writers for quality (odds ratio 5.42), 28 MFA-trained readers also preferred them (odds ratio 1.87), detectors flagged only 3 percent as AI, and the median fine-tuning cost was $81 per author.
bottom_line: Strong signal on both quality and cost, tempered by being a preprint that tested excerpts of up to 450 words rather than whole novels.

text: In a preregistered experiment with 254 participants, labeling short stories as AI-written, human-written or unlabeled produced no reliable differences in ratings of creativity, enjoyment, recommendation or originality, although readers guessed human-labeled stories took about 148 minutes to write versus 6 minutes for AI-labeled ones.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it suggests labels may not sink AI fiction, but it is small, uses 200-word stories, and found that perceived effort still shaped enjoyment.

text: Of 69 professional translators who read three Italian short stories, two by ChatGPT-4o and one by a human, only about 16.2 percent reliably told which were machine-generated.
bottom_line: Some weight: even trained language professionals struggle to spot AI fiction, though the sample and the number of stories are small.

text: A novel whose publisher discloses that most of its text was generated by AI will appear on the weekly New York Times fiction bestseller list.

At least one of the five largest U.S. trade publishers (Penguin Random House, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, Hachette or Macmillan) will publish a novel whose text it says was generated mainly by AI.
A novel disclosed as mainly AI-generated sells more than one million copies in the United States within a year of release, according to Circana BookScan or the publisher.
A large, representative survey finds that most U.S. fiction buyers would knowingly buy an AI-written novel at the same price as a human-written one in their favorite genre.
Most novel buyers choose books by price, genre and cover rather than by who or what wrote the text.
AI language models will keep improving over the next ten years at something close to the pace of the last five years.
Sales of AI-written novels will be counted in a way that separates them from human-written novels, so that a claim of outselling can actually be checked.
Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, posted in March 2025 that a short story written by an unreleased OpenAI model was the first time he had been really struck by something written by AI.

Stephen Marche, a Canadian novelist and journalist, produced the 2023 crime novella Death of an Author largely from AI-generated text and published it through Pushkin Industries under the pen name Aidan Marchine.
AI-generated poetry is indistinguishable from human-written poetry and is rated more favorably, Brian Porter and Edouard Machery, 2024
bridge: In blind tests, ordinary readers could not reliably tell AI poems from poems by well-known poets and rated the AI poems more favorably, which supports the claim that readers buying blind would not avoid AI writing.
bottom_line: Real weight on reader detection and taste, but poems are short and the study says nothing about whether people would buy a whole AI-written novel.

text: Readers Prefer Outputs of AI Trained on Copyrighted Books over Expert Human Writers, Tuhin Chakrabarty, Jane C. Ginsburg and Paramveer Dhillon, 2025
bridge: When AI models were fine-tuned on the books of 50 award-winning authors, both MFA-trained and general readers preferred the AI excerpts (up to 450 words) to excerpts by expert human writers, AI detectors flagged only 3 percent of them, and fine-tuning cost a median of $81 per author.
bottom_line: Strong weight on cost and short-passage quality, but it is a preprint, the excerpts are short, and the same study found expert readers strongly preferred humans when the AI was only prompted, not fine-tuned.

text: Readers buy novels largely out of loyalty to particular authors, so name-brand human novelists will keep most sales even if AI prose matches theirs.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: bestseller lists are dominated by returning author names, though this loyalty is weaker for readers who binge cheap series.

text: Text generated solely by AI cannot be copyrighted in the United States, so publishers have little reason to spend marketing money on novels anyone could legally copy and resell.
bottom_line: Strong weight for traditional publishers, though it does little to stop self-publishers and leaves room for AI-assisted books with enough human expression.

text: Outselling human-written novels requires AI-written novels to win more than half of all novel sales, a far higher bar than flooding retailers with new titles.
bottom_line: Heavy weight: it separates the easy part (many titles) from the hard part (most sales), which is what the belief actually claims.

text: Long novels still expose AI weaknesses in plot, originality and coherence over hundreds of pages that short blind tests do not measure.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: expert tests support it today, but it is the weakness most likely to shrink within ten years.

text: Many readers, booksellers and prize committees treat AI authorship as a reason to reject a book, and human-authorship labels make that rejection easy to act on.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: surveys show people want to know who made a work, but whether that changes purchases at scale is not yet measured for novels.

text: Books where a person directs and heavily edits AI drafts will usually be counted as human-written, leaving few best-selling novels that clearly qualify as AI-written.
bottom_line: Heavy weight on how the belief resolves: the more AI is blended into human authorship, the less likely any count shows AI-written novels in the lead.

text: When creative writing experts judged stories with the Torrance Test of Creative Writing, stories generated by large language models passed 3 to 10 times fewer of the tests than stories written by professionals.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: expert judges found a large gap in originality and craft, though it tested 2023-era models and the same lead author later found fine-tuning narrowed the gap.

text: Across six experiments with nearly 3,000 participants, people devalued art labeled as AI-made on many dimensions, even when they said it was indistinguishable from human-made art.
bottom_line: Moderate weight by analogy: it shows a real penalty for the AI label, but it studied visual art, and a 2026 fiction study did not find the same penalty.

text: In a survey of 5,023 U.S. adults taken June 9 to 15, 2025, 76 percent said it is extremely or very important to be able to tell whether pictures, videos and text were made by AI or by people, and 53 percent said AI will worsen people's ability to think creatively.
bottom_line: Some weight: Americans clearly want to know who made a work, but wanting a label is not the same as refusing to buy a labeled AI novel.

text: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld in 2025 the Copyright Office's refusal to register a work generated solely by a machine, and by March 2026 the Supreme Court had declined to hear challenges to that position.
bottom_line: Strong weight for traditional publishing economics, since uncopyrightable novels are hard to invest in, though it does not stop low-cost self-publishing.

text: Amazon's year-end list of the most-sold Kindle fiction titles will include no novel disclosed or credibly reported as mainly AI-generated in any year through 2030.
Labels certifying human authorship, such as the Authors Guild's Human Authored mark, will appear on the listings or covers of a majority of new novels from the five largest U.S. trade publishers.
Sales data show that books disclosed as AI-generated stay below 1 percent of U.S. fiction units for several years even as their share of new titles rises.
After a major retailer begins showing an AI-generated label on book listings, sales of the labeled novels fall sharply compared with similar unlabeled novels.
Many readers value a novel partly because a particular person wrote it, and that value does not disappear when the AI prose gets better.
Retailers, publishers or lawmakers will require clear labels for AI-written books well before ten years have passed.
Most commercially successful novels that use AI will have enough human writing and editing to be counted as human-written.
Ted Chiang, the science fiction author, argued in The New Yorker in 2024 that AI text generators are not going to make art, because art depends on the many choices a person makes while creating it.
Art or Artifice? Large Language Models and the False Promise of Creativity, Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban, Divyansh Agarwal, Smaranda Muresan and Chien-Sheng Wu, 2024
where_found: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (ACM)
bridge: Ten creative-writing experts judged 48 stories on 14 craft tests and found that stories generated by large language models passed three to ten times fewer tests than stories by professional writers.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: it measures the craft gap directly with expert judges, but it tested 2023 models on short stories, and the gap may close.

text: Readers of fast-release series fiction, such as romance and fantasy fans, need a steady supply of new books in the subgenres they love.
measured_by: Number of new titles per year in their favorite subgenres and the average wait between installments of a series.
if_true: New titles rise sharply and the wait between installments shrinks.
if_false: Release pace stays limited by how fast human authors can write.
bottom_line: A real and sizable group whose buying habits are the most likely path for AI novels to gain sales.

text: Readers on tight budgets need novels they can afford.
measured_by: Average price of a new ebook novel and the number of novels bought per reader per year.
if_true: Prices for new novels fall and low-income readers buy more of them.
if_false: Prices stay near today's levels, set by human writing and editing costs.
bottom_line: Moderate: cheap self-published ebooks already exist, so the extra gain from AI pricing may be small.

text: Working novelists need book sales to pay their bills.
measured_by: Median income novelists earn from books, as tracked by author income surveys such as the Authors Guild's.
if_true: Median book income falls as AI novels take sales.
if_false: Book income holds steady or rises as human authorship becomes a selling point.
bottom_line: The group with the most to lose, and its organized response, through lawsuits and labels, is itself one reason the belief may fail.

text: Readers who care who wrote a book need honest labels showing whether a person or an AI wrote it.
measured_by: Share of retail book listings that show buyers a clear AI-generated or human-authored label.
if_true: Labels stay rare or hidden while AI novels take most sales.
if_false: Clear labels become common and readers use them to choose human-written books.
bottom_line: Large in number per the 2025 Pew survey, and decisive if labels become visible at the point of sale.

text: Independent booksellers need books by human authors who can tour, sign and talk with readers.
measured_by: Independent bookstore fiction sales and the number of author events they host each year.
if_true: Fiction sales and author events at independent stores decline.
if_false: Independent stores keep or grow their fiction sales and events.
bottom_line: Moderate: a smaller share of total sales, but an important channel for building the author loyalty that works against the belief.

text: Publishers could produce a novel-length manuscript in an established author's style for a small fraction of what they now pay writers.
bottom_line: The cost figure comes from one 2025 preprint's estimate of fine-tuning versus typical writer pay, and it leaves out editing, marketing and legal costs.

text: Readers of long-running series could get new installments in their favorite subgenres far faster than human authors can write them.
bottom_line: A real gain for heavy genre readers, though more titles also means more work sorting good books from bad.

text: Novels could become cheaper, letting readers with little money buy more of them.
bottom_line: Plausible given production costs, but no data yet show retail prices for AI novels falling below today's low-cost self-published ebooks.

text: Working novelists would lose much of their book income as AI-written novels take over sales they now earn.
bottom_line: The largest cost if the belief comes true, and the reason authors' groups are fighting it, though its size depends on how much of the market AI wins.

text: Online bookstores would fill with low-effort AI titles, making it harder for readers to find books worth their time and money.
bottom_line: Already visible on a small scale, as when Clarkesworld closed submissions in 2023 after AI spam surged, and likely to grow with volume.

text: Fake books sold under real authors' names would multiply, as when AI-made titles were listed under writer Jane Friedman's name on Amazon and Goodreads in 2023.
bottom_line: A real harm to authors and buyers, though platforms can reduce it with identity checks regardless of how much AI fiction sells.

text: Independent bookstores would lose the author readings, signings and hand-selling that set them apart from online retailers.
bottom_line: Moderate weight: bookstores could keep stocking human authors, but would suffer if most fiction sales moved to cheap AI titles sold online.

text: Whether novels whose text was mainly generated by AI account for more than half of U.S. novel units sold in any 12-month period ending by October 4, 2036 is a fair measure of whether AI-written novels outsold human-written novels within ten years.

The share of titles disclosed as AI-generated among the top 100 sellers on Amazon's annual Kindle fiction list is a fair measure of whether AI-written novels are winning readers rather than only filling catalogs.
The gap between AI-generated novels' share of new fiction titles and their share of fiction sales is a fair measure of whether readers buy AI novels or merely find them on shelves.
Within ten years, AI language models will be able to write full-length novels that ordinary readers enjoy as much as typical human-written novels in the same genre.
Lower production costs and faster release schedules for AI-written novels will translate into more total sales, not just more titles on sale.
Sales of novels can be reliably sorted into AI-written and human-written, so that the AI share can be measured against more than half of all novel sales.
The number of AI-written novels listed on major ebook platforms such as Amazon Kindle would rise sharply, mostly in romance, fantasy and other fast-release genres.
Prices for new ebook novels in the most crowded genres would fall as AI-written titles compete with human-written ones for the same readers.
Median income that working novelists earn from book sales would fall as AI-written novels take more than half of novel sales.
Publishers and booksellers would build a separate, premium market for novels certified as written by people, similar to the market for handmade goods.
AI-written novels will outsell human-written novels within five years.
Within ten years, almost no new best-selling novels will be written primarily by people.
AI-written novels will outsell human-written novels in at least one major genre, such as romance, within ten years.
AI-written novels will make up at least a tenth of all novel sales within ten years.
Video games are an art form on a level with film and literature.
bottom_line: The record that video games are a form of creative expression is strong: the Supreme Court, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Smithsonian and the Grammys all treat them that way. Whether the medium has reached the level of film and literature rests mostly on critics' judgment, with no blind comparison and no recent poll asking the question directly, so the real fight is over what counts as art and whether a medium is judged by its best works or its best-sellers.
hook: In 2012 an estimated 680,000 people visited the Smithsonian American Art Museum's exhibition The Art of Video Games, after 119,000 people in 175 countries cast more than 3.7 million votes to choose the games it showed.
question: Are video games an art form on a level with film and literature?
ask: The page most needs a published study or recent national poll that measures whether critics or the public, judging the same way, rate acclaimed video games as highly as acclaimed films and novels.

text: Video games tell stories with the same tools film and literature use (characters, dialogue, plot and music) and add one tool neither older form has: the player's own choices.
bottom_line: Strong as a reason games can be art at all, since the U.S. Supreme Court used this exact reasoning in 2011, but it shows games have the tools of art, not that they have matched the best films and novels.

text: Interactivity lets a video game make the player feel responsible for a character's actions, an effect a reader or viewer watching from outside a story cannot get in the same way.
bottom_line: Moderate: this is the best case that games can do something film and literature cannot, but how often games actually achieve it is a matter of critical judgment, not measurement.

text: Film was widely treated as cheap commercial entertainment in its first decades before critics accepted it as an art form, so the low standing of a young medium says little about what it can become.
bottom_line: Moderate: the historical pattern is real and should make critics cautious, but a past case of a medium rising does not prove video games will rise the same way.

text: Major cultural institutions, including the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the Museum of Modern Art, the National Endowment for the Arts and the Recording Academy, now exhibit, collect, fund or give awards to video games as creative works.
bottom_line: Fairly strong, because these are independent bodies with reputations to protect, though several of them treat games as design or music rather than as art equal to film and literature.

text: A major video game combines the work of visual artists, writers, actors, composers and designers, so a single game can contain several recognized art forms at once.
bottom_line: Moderate: it shows games are full of artistic labor, but a container of art forms is not automatically an artwork on the level of its best parts.

text: Governments in France and Germany have formally treated video games as cultural works, with France giving its arts honor, the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, to game designers in 2006.
bottom_line: Moderate: official recognition shows the claim is taken seriously by cultural authorities, though governments also have industrial and tax reasons to praise a profitable sector.

text: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association that video games get full First Amendment protection, with the majority opinion saying that like protected books, plays and movies, they communicate ideas through familiar literary devices and features distinctive to the medium.
bottom_line: Strong evidence that U.S. law treats games as expression on the same footing as film and books, though legal protection covers bad art and non-art alike, so it does not settle artistic rank.

text: The Smithsonian American Art Museum's exhibition The Art of Video Games, which ran from March 16 to September 30, 2012, drew an estimated 680,000 visitors, after more than 3.7 million votes from 119,000 people in 175 countries chose the games it showed.
bottom_line: Good evidence that a national art museum and a large public treat games as worth exhibiting as art, though attendance measures interest, not artistic level.

text: A national poll of U.S. adults will find that a majority agree video games can be art as much as films and books.
At least one major art museum that has acquired video games will place a game in its film, media art or fine art department rather than its design department.
A blind study finds that critics who do not review games rate scenes from acclaimed video games as highly as scenes from acclaimed films and novels on artistic merit.
A study finds that players remember and reflect on the moral themes of narrative video games as deeply and for as long as readers of comparable novels.
An art form should be judged by its best works rather than by its average or best-selling products, as film and literature already are.
A player's choices inside a video game can serve the expression of a designer's vision instead of destroying it.
Artistic merit can be compared across different art forms, so it makes sense to say a video game is on a level with a great film or novel.

Justice Antonin Scalia wrote for the U.S. Supreme Court majority in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association (2011) that video games, like the books, plays and movies before them, communicate ideas through familiar literary devices such as characters, dialogue, plot and music, and so qualify for First Amendment protection.
Kellee Santiago, co-founder of the game studio thatgamecompany, argued in a 2009 TEDxUSC talk that video games are already art, and that talk prompted Roger Ebert's 2010 column disputing her.

Paola Antonelli, senior curator at the Museum of Modern Art, wrote in 2012 when MoMA added fourteen video games to its collection that video games are art but are also design, and that MoMA chose to collect them as design.
Games: Agency as Art, C. Thi Nguyen, 2020
bridge: Philosopher C. Thi Nguyen argues that games are a distinct art form whose medium is agency itself, letting designers shape how players act and strive in the way novels shape what readers imagine.
bottom_line: Strong for the claim that games are an art form with their own unique material, though it argues games are a different kind of art rather than ranking them against film and literature.

text: The Art of Videogames, Grant Tavinor, 2009
bridge: Grant Tavinor applies the standard philosophical definitions of art to video games and concludes that many of them qualify as art by those same tests.
bottom_line: Moderate to strong: a careful academic case that games meet the definitions of art, though meeting a definition is a lower bar than matching the best films and novels.

text: The Art of Video Games: From Pac-Man to Mass Effect, Chris Melissinos and Patrick O'Rourke, 2012
where_found: Welcome Books, companion to the Smithsonian American Art Museum exhibition of the same name
bridge: The companion book to the 2012 Smithsonian American Art Museum exhibition presents forty years of video games as a visual and narrative art form chosen in part by public vote.
bottom_line: Moderate: it documents a major art museum treating games as art, but it is a celebratory exhibition catalog written by the exhibition's own curator, not a neutral assessment.

text: Most video games are built around goals, rules, scores and winning, which makes them closer to chess or sports than to a novel or a film, as film critic Roger Ebert argued in 2010.
bottom_line: Strong against games in general, since most best-sellers really are contests, but weak against the narrower claim that some games are art, and Ebert himself softened his position later in 2010.

text: Handing control of a story to the player weakens authorship, so a video game cannot shape a person's experience as precisely as a novelist or film director shapes theirs.
bottom_line: Moderate: it names a real tradeoff, but it assumes art requires one controlling author, which theater, jazz and architecture already challenge.

text: The best-selling video games in the United States are mostly yearly sports titles and shooter sequels designed to keep people playing and paying, which shows the medium is driven mainly by commerce rather than expression.
bottom_line: Moderate: the sales lists support it, but the best-selling films are mostly sequels too, and film is still judged by its best work rather than its biggest hits.

text: After about fifty years, video games still lack a body of works that critics outside gaming widely rank alongside the great novels and films.
bottom_line: Fairly strong as the central question of the page, though film had fewer than fifty years behind it when critics began to canonize it, and the claim is hard to test without a survey of critics.

text: Museums that collect video games, such as the Museum of Modern Art, have mostly filed them as interaction design rather than as fine art, which treats them as well-made objects rather than artworks equal to films and novels.
bottom_line: Moderate: the filing is a fact, but curators chose it partly because the design department is where interactive objects already lived, so it may reflect museum structure more than a verdict on merit.

text: In a 2015 national survey, 26% of American adults said most video games are a waste of time.
bottom_line: Modest: it shows a sizable minority of the public does not see games as serious culture, but it is a decade old and did not ask about art directly.

text: Seven of the ten best-selling premium games in the United States in 2024 were yearly sports titles or Call of Duty releases, led by Call of Duty: Black Ops 6.
bottom_line: Moderate evidence that the commercial center of the medium is repeat franchises, though it says nothing about the artistic level of the medium's best works.

text: Among U.S. adult players, 68% said they play to pass time or relax and 62% to have fun, the top two reasons given.
bottom_line: Weak to modest: it suggests most play is pastime rather than an encounter with art, but most people also watch films and read books to relax.

text: When the Museum of Modern Art acquired its first 14 video games in 2012, it placed them in its Architecture and Design department, the department that collects designed objects, rather than with its film or fine art collections.
bottom_line: Modest: the placement suggests the museum valued games as design, though the museum has a film department and chose not to use it, which could reflect how games are made rather than how good they are.

text: No published blind comparison by critics outside gaming will rate acclaimed video games as highly, on average, as acclaimed films and novels from the same decade.
National polls of U.S. adults will continue to find fewer than half saying video games are art on the level of film and literature, even as the share of adults who play keeps rising.
A survey of critics from film, literature and the visual arts finds that almost none would rank any video game among the hundred most important artworks of the past fifty years.
A survey of game developers finds that most describe their own work as building a product or service rather than expressing something, as Hideo Kojima did in 2006.
A work of art needs a single author, or a small group, who controls exactly what the audience experiences.
An activity organized around goals, rules and winning is a game in the same sense as chess or sports, whatever pictures, music and story are attached to it.
A medium earns a place beside film and literature only after a broad body of critics outside its own fans ranks particular works alongside the great films and novels.

Film critic Roger Ebert wrote in 2010 that video games can never be art, and although he later that year conceded he should not have said never about games he had not played, he said he still believed games were not art in principle.

Guardian art critic Jonathan Jones wrote in 2012, responding to the Museum of Modern Art's video game acquisitions, that video games are not art because no single person's vision of life shapes a game the player controls.

Game designer and professor Brian Moriarty argued in a 2011 Game Developers Conference lecture titled An Apology for Roger Ebert that Ebert was right that video games do not reach the sublime art found in the greatest works of painting, music and literature.
Sorry MoMA, video games are not art, Jonathan Jones, 2012
bridge: Art critic Jonathan Jones argued that because a game's world is shaped by the player's choices, no single artist's personal vision is expressed, so games are not art even when well made.
bottom_line: Moderate: a clear statement of the authorship objection from a working art critic, though it rests on the disputed premise that art needs one controlling author.

text: Video Games Are Better Without Stories, Ian Bogost, 2017
bridge: Game scholar and designer Ian Bogost argued that games that imitate film and literature tend to tell weaker stories than those forms, and that games do their best work through systems and spaces instead.
bottom_line: Moderate: it comes from a defender of games and cuts against the comparison to film and literature rather than against games being art at all.

text: Game developers and writers need their work treated as serious creative expression so it can win arts funding, legal protection and critical attention.
measured_by: Number of arts grants, general-interest arts reviews and cultural awards given to video games each year.
if_true: The counts rise toward those given to independent films and literary fiction.
if_false: The counts stay flat or limited to game-industry awards.
bottom_line: A strong and direct interest, since the label changes who will fund and review the work.

text: Museum curators and archivists need institutional backing to preserve old video games before the hardware that runs them disappears.
measured_by: Number of historically significant games held in playable form by public museums, libraries and archives.
if_true: Preservation budgets and collections grow as games are treated like films.
if_false: More early games become unplayable as original hardware fails.
bottom_line: A real interest that does not depend on games matching the best films, only on their being worth keeping.

text: Teenage players need the pastime that most of them share, video games, taken seriously by parents and teachers rather than dismissed as wasted time.
measured_by: Share of parents and teachers in surveys who say games can have educational or artistic value.
if_true: The share rises and games appear in some school lessons.
if_false: Games remain treated mainly as a distraction to limit.
bottom_line: Meaningful given how many teens play, though respect for a pastime does not require ranking it with literature.
